## See the Collection Before Writing Its Loop

A store records quantities for four delivery slots. Four unrelated variables would require four separate names and repeated processing code. An array gives the values one name and a position-based organization. Its length is fixed when the array object is created; its elements can still change. This connects the collection idea to variables: assignment changes a value in a particular slot, while a loop chooses which slot to visit.

Use these schematic forms to distinguish three actions:

```text
elementType[] name;                         // Declare a variable for an array reference.
name = new elementType[lengthExpression];    // Create an array and store its reference.
name[indexExpression] = valueExpression;    // Replace one element of that array.
```

`[]` after the type describes the array type. Brackets after a variable name select an element. Length counts elements; an index identifies a position. For four slots, the valid indexes are zero through three. Index four is already outside the array.

The first line shows default values after allocation. The later assignment reads indexes one and three, computes `4 * 5 - 6`, and stores 14 at index two. It does not insert a fifth quantity or change the array's length.

| Index | After allocation | After four assignments | After the calculation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 0 | 7 | 7 |
| 1 | 0 | 5 | 5 |
| 2 | 0 | 9 | 14 |
| 3 | 0 | 6 | 6 |

Read the table by column to see a whole array state, or by row to follow one element. The loop's condition checks `index < quantities.Length` before each read. The semicolons in a for header separate initialization, condition and update. A comma between condition and update is not the syntax for this loop.

An initializer such as `int[] quantities = { 7, 5, 9, 6 };` creates the same four initial values more compactly. Use `foreach` when only the values matter; use an index when the task selects or changes positions. A foreach loop can stop early with `break`, but it does not directly provide the current position for an indexed update.

```

## Guide a Last-Element Check

The comparison is `>`. For an empty array, evaluating index -1 would be invalid, so the read occurs only inside the guarded branch. For one element, Length is one and its last index is zero. As a variation, change only the second slot in the four-element example and predict the entire new state before running it. The retained examples below add other loop forms, string arrays, returned arrays, defaults and library operations.
```{index} 1D Arrays ```

```{index} array; [ ] declaration
```

An array is a **collection type** and a `data structure` that contains a number of variables that are accessed
through computed indices. The variables contained in an array, also called the
`elements` of the array, are all of the same type, and this type is called the
`element type` of the array. [1]

In C#, an array is a structure representing a **fixed length** `ordered` collection of
values or objects with the **same type**. Arrays make it easier to organize and
operate on large amounts of data. For example, rather than creating 100 integer
variables, you can just create one array that stores all those integers and access
them using array indices. [2]

You have learned that a string is an immutable `sequence` of characters and how to
loop through the sequence. Arrays provide more general sequences, with the
same indexing notation, but with free choice of the `type` of the items in the
sequence, and the ability to `change` the elements in the sequence.


The collection idea connects this chapter to the next one. An array supplies an ordered group of elements, indexed access, and traversal, but its length stays fixed after creation. A `List<T>` supports a changing number of elements; a dictionary retrieves values by key; a set represents distinct values; and stacks, queues, and priority queues select the next item by a processing rule. You do not need their syntax yet. First learn the array operations here, then compare the broader families in {doc}`Data Collections <../08_collections/0801_collections>`. The separate chapters mark a learning sequence, not a boundary between arrays and collections.

```{index} Creating Arrays
```

```{index} Creating Arrays
```

## Creating Arrays

A C# `array variable` is declared similarly to a non-array variable, with the
addition of square brackets (`[]`) after the `type` specifier to denote it as an array.
So, the general form for declaring an array variable of the element type is:

> **type**`[]` variableName;

For example, if you want to create an array called `a` with the type `int`
for elements, you declare the array variable as:

    int[] a;

In this declaration, you do *not* know how many elements will be in this array
from the preceding declaration. You must give further information to create the
corresponding `array object`. A new object can be created using the `new`
syntax. An array must get a definite length, which can be a literal integer or
any integer expression. The general syntax to create a new array is

> `new` **type**`[` *length* `]`

After the type, there are square brackets enclosing an expression for the length
of the array - this length is unchangeable after creation. For example

    int[] a;
    a = new int[4];

or, you may combine with the declaration,

    int[] a = new int[4];

to creates an array that holds 4 integers. After specifying the number of the elements
of the array, the default initial values are also assigned. For example, numerical
arrays get initialized to all 0’s (false for boolean, the character with Unicode
number zero for char, and null for objects and string) with this syntax by default, so when you loop
through the array variable:

    > foreach (int i in a)
      {
          Console.Write(i);
      }
    0000
    >

An **array initializer** consists of a sequence of variable initializers,
enclosed by “`{`” and”`}`” tokens and separated by “`,`” tokens.
An array initializer can be used in a variable declaration:

    int[] a = {0, 2, 4, 6, 8};

which is a shorthand for the equivalent `array creation expression`:

    int[] a = new int[] {0, 2, 4, 6, 8};

Note that the actual data for an array is *not* stored directly in the memory location
allocated by the declaration. The array could have any number of items, and hence
the memory requirements are not known at compile time. Like all other object
(as opposed to primitive) types, what is actually stored at the memory location declared
for `a` is a *reference* to the actual place where the data for the array is stored.
In actual compiler implementation, this reference is an address in memory. In the diagram
below, you see the object references with an arrow *pointing* to the actual location
for the object’s data after `a` is initialized:

```{figure} ../../figures/newArray1.png
:alt: new array
:width: 300px

New array.
```

The small box beside `a` is meant to indicate the memory space allocated when `a` is
declared. As you can see that space does not actually contain the array, but rather a
*reference* to the array, pointing to the actual sequence of data for the array.
Also, in the diagram you see the indices associated with each element, though they
are not actual a part of what is stored in memory.

## Default Initializations

Did you notice that when the first example array of integers was created,
it was filled with zeros? It is a safety feature of C# that the internal fields
of objects always get a specific value, not random data. Here are the defaults:

| Type | Default element value |
| --- | --- |
| Primitive numeric types | 0 |
| bool | false |
| Reference types, including string | null |

```{warning}
An array with elements of reference type, like `string[]`, without a specific initializer
gets initialized to all null values. Array creation is legal, but reading a member of a null element fails.
```

This intentionally failing fragment illustrates the missing-element problem:

```csharp
string[] words = new string[10];
Console.WriteLine(words[0].Length); // Runtime error: this element is null.
```

The error is because null is not an object and has no Length property.
If you want an array of empty strings, initialize the elements with a loop:

```csharp
string[] words = new string[10];
for (int i = 0; i < words.Length; i++) {
    words[i] = "";
}

```{index} LINQ Methods
```

## LINQ Methods

Language-Integrated Query (LINQ) is a set of technologies integrating query capabilities into C#. The full query topic is later reading; these calls are library aggregation examples.

All C# array types derive from System.Array. Arrays provide enumeration, which permits LINQ extension calls such as Max(), Min(), Sum() and Reverse() when the appropriate namespace is imported. Reverse() produces a sequence rather than automatically changing the original array.

```csharp
using System.Linq;
int[] nums = new int[5] { 10, 15, 16, 8, 6 };
nums.Max();     // Returns 16.
nums.Min();     // Returns 6.
nums.Sum();     // Returns 55.
nums.Average(); // Returns 11.
```

The average is 55 divided by five. These fragments illustrate result values; they do not print them. The complete runnable examples earlier show how to display results.

**Check the library-method summary:** The five values 10, 15, 16, 8 and 6 have sum 55, so their average is 55 / 5 = 11. The Average result comment above is corrected to 11. Sum and Average are different aggregation contracts, even when both consume the same values. The array-processing lesson supplies complete runnable loop examples.
The array declarations and initialization forms above follow these references.[^arrays-specification][^arrays-cheatsheet]

```

# Arrays

A week of sales figures is easier to process as one indexed group than as seven unrelated variables. An array is a collection type with a fixed length. This chapter connects element access and loop traversal to aggregation, shared references, method calls, and rectangular data; Chapter 8 broadens the choice of collection families.

- **Array**: An array stores a fixed number of same-typed values under one name.
- **Index**: An index selects a specific element by position.
- **Traversal**: Loops let a program visit each array element systematically.
- **Two-dimensional array**: A 2D array models grid-like data such as tables, boards, and matrices.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Explain why an array is a collection, then declare, initialize, and access one-dimensional arrays within their valid index ranges.
2. Traverse arrays with `for` and `foreach` to calculate results and update elements where appropriate.
3. Trace array reference assignment and distinguish sharing from making a separate shallow copy.
4. Pass arrays to methods and return array results while explaining which operations can change the caller's elements.
5. Declare and process rectangular arrays using the correct bounds for each dimension.

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Array | A fixed-size collection of values stored in indexed order. |
| 2 | Element | One value stored inside an array. |
| 3 | Index | A zero-based position used to access an array element. |
| 4 | Length | The number of elements an array can hold. |
| 5 | Initializer | Syntax that creates an array with starting values. |
| 6 | Traversal | Visiting each element in a collection. |
| 7 | For loop traversal | Array processing that uses an index variable. |
| 8 | Foreach traversal | Array processing that visits each element directly. |
| 9 | Bounds | The valid index range from `0` through `Length - 1`. |
| 10 | Out-of-range error | An error caused by using an invalid index. |
| 11 | Two-dimensional array | A rectangular array addressed by row and column indexes. |
| 12 | Row | A horizontal group of values in a two-dimensional array. |
| 13 | Column | A vertical group of values in a two-dimensional array. |
| 14 | Array parameter | A method parameter whose value is an array reference. |
| 15 | Alias | Another reference to the same array object. |
| 16 | Shallow copy | A separate array containing copied element values or references, without cloning referenced objects. |
| 17 | Rectangular array | An array with a fixed length for each dimension and the same row width throughout. |

## Process Positions Before Introducing a New Container

An array gives many values one shared organization. To calculate a total, the program still needs a rule for visiting those values and combining them. The accumulator pattern connects arrays to Chapter 4: initialize a running result, visit each relevant element, and update the result exactly once for that element. The array changes where input values come from; it does not change the meaning of a loop or an assignment.

Suppose daily quantities are 4, 0 and 7. Before the first iteration the total is zero because no entries have been processed. After each iteration, total should equal the sum of the processed prefix. This claim explains both the initialization and the update. It also provides a way to find a defect before the final result is printed.

| Processed positions | Next position | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 4 |
| 0 and 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 0 through 2 | End | 11 |

A for loop exposes positions and is useful when you must report an index or replace elements. A foreach loop exposes each element value directly and is useful when only those values matter. Do not assume that changing a foreach iteration variable updates an array element. Use explicit indexing when the operation is defined in terms of changing positions.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

```{index} Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements
```

```{index} Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements
```

## Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements

A method parameter of type int[] receives a copy of the reference value. Caller and helper can therefore refer to the same array. Replacing an element through the helper is visible through the caller's reference. Reassigning the helper's parameter to a different array changes that local parameter, not the caller's variable. This connects ordinary parameter passing from Chapter 5 with reference aliasing, without requiring pass-by-reference parameter syntax.

State whether a processing helper may mutate its input. A Total helper normally only reads values. An ApplyAdjustment helper might intentionally replace them. If a reporting task must preserve original values, computing into another array or returning a separate result is a different contract from modifying the original and restoring it afterward.

An empty array is a real collection with Length zero. A total over no quantities naturally returns zero under the sum contract. A request for the first element has no valid result on that same input. Handle the operation's domain rather than giving every array helper the same empty-case behavior. A null reference is different again: there is no array object whose Length can be read.

Guided exercise: replace the quantities with 0, 0 and 7. Predict the accumulator trace. Then predict the result for an empty array. Finally, explain whether the read-only total should change if another variable is assigned the array reference. An alias alone changes no element, but a later mutation through either alias can change what a subsequent total reads.

## Parameters to Main

The `Main` method may take an array of strings as parameter, as in this example:

```csharp
/// Demonstrate the use of command line parameters.
static void Main(string[] args)
{
   Console.WriteLine("There are {0} command line parameters.", args.Length);
   foreach(string s in args) {
      Console.WriteLine(s);
   }

}
```

By convention, the formal parameter for `Main` is called `args`,
short for arguments.

Compile (`dotnet build`) and run (`dotnet run`) the program from the command line.
Run it with some things at the end of the line in `macOS` like:

``` none
[username]@[computer]:~/workspace/introcscs/Ch08Arrays$ dotnet run hi there 123
```

or in `Windows` like:

``` none
PS C:\Users\[username]\workspace\introcscs\Ch08Arrays> dotnet run hi there 123
```

and it should print for you:

``` none
There are 3 command line parameters.
hi
there
123
```

See what quoted strings do. Use command line parameters (with the quotes)
`"hi there" 123`. This should print for you:

    There are 2 command line parameters.
    hi there

### Command Line Adder

A code block in the Main method of your project that calculates and prints
the sum of three command line parameters taken from user input:

    2 5 22

then the program prints 29.

The code could look like this:

    ////////// args array from command line.
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < args.Length; i++)
    {
          sum = sum + int.Parse(args[i]);
    }
    Console.WriteLine(sum);

Here we are using the `arg` array directly just like the preceding section.

To run the code this time, go down to your project’s bin/Debug/net8.0 directory
from the command line, and run `ls`. You will find the executables (the `.dll` or `.exe`
files) that you can execute. In `Windows`, it should look like:

``` none
PS C:\Users\[username]\workspace\introcscs\Ch08Arrays\bin\Debug\net8.0> Ch08Arrays.exe 2 5 22
```

and you will see the output. You can also run the project by issuing:

``` none
PS C:\Users\[username]\workspace\introcscs\Ch08Arrays> dotnet run 2 5 22
```

as before to see the same output. In earlier version of `macOS`, you run this
with `dotnet run` in your project folder at command line with the arguments:

``` none
[username]@[computer]:~/workspace/introcscs/Ch08Arrays$ dotnet run 2 5 22
```

or in more current versions of `macOS`:

``` none
[username]@[computer]:~/workspace/introcscs/Ch08Arrays/bin/Debug/net8.0$ dotnet Ch08Arrays.dll 2 5 22
```

and you will see the output of the sum of the integers.

Just like the preceding section, this shows that the `string[] args` in the Main method is a `string array` taking its
elements from the command line when the project is executed in the command line with arguments provided.

(alias)=

## References and Aliases

Object variables, like arrays, are references,
and this has important implications for
assignment.

With a primitive type like an `int`, an assignment copies the data:

`{image} ../../figures/intCopy.png :align: center :alt: copying an int :width: 90 pt`

In the diagram, the contents of the memory box labeled `b` is copied to the
memory box labeled `d`. The value of `d` starts off equal to the value of `b`,
but can later be changed independently.

Contrast an assignment with arrays. The value that is copied is the *reference*,
not the array data itself, so both end up pointing at the *same* actual array:

`{image} ../../figures/arrayAlias.png :align: center :alt: copying an array reference :width: 300 pt`

Hereafter, array assignments like:

    b[2] = -10;
    d[1] = 55;

would both change the *same* array. Now `b` and `d` are essentially
names for the same thing (the actual array). The technical term matches English:
The names are *aliases*.

This may seem like a pretty silly discussion. Why bother to give two different
names to the same object? Isn’t one enough? In fact it is very important
in function/method calls. An array reference can be passed as an actual value,
and it is the array *reference* that is copied to the formal parameter, so
the formal parameter name is an **alias** for the actual parameter name.

If an array passed as a parameter to a method has elements changed in the
method, then the change affects the actual parameter array.
The change *remains* in the actual parameter array *after*
the method has terminated.

```{index} array; Scale example
```

For example, consider the following function:

    // Modify a by multiplying all elements by multiplier.
    static void Scale(int[] a, int multiplier)
    {
       for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) {
          a[i] *= multiplier;  // or:  a[i] = a[i] * multiplier
       }
    }

The fragment:

    int[] nums = {2, 4, 1};
    Scale(nums, 5);

would *change* nums, so it ends up containing elements 10, 20, and 5.

An array can have any number of dimensions. For example, one-dimension (1D), 2-dimension
(2D), 3-dimension (3D) as shown below [^0702_twodim-multi-d-arrays].

> ```{image} ../../figures/multi-d-arrays.jpg

Since arrays use indices to access the elements, you must specify the
indexing position within the array for data manipulation.
In a 1d array you specify just the index, in a 2d array,
you specify row and column, and in a 3d array you specify plane, row, and column.
You can have higher dimension arrays, but they are just difficult to imagine.

## Rectangular Arrays (Two Dimensional)

While a one-dimensional array works for a sequence of data,
you need something more for a two dimensional table,
where data values vary over both row and column.

If we have a table of integers, for instance with three
rows and four columns:

```
2 4  7 55
3 1  8 10
6 0 49 12
```

We could declare an array variable of the right size as
int[,] table = new int[3, 4];

Multiple indices are separated by commas inside the square brackets.
In declaring an array type, no indices are included so the `[,]`
indicates a two dimensional array. Where the `new` object is being created,
the values inside the square brackets give each dimension.

In general the notation for a two dimensional array declaration is:

> **type** `[, ]` **variableName**

and to create a new array with default values:

> new **type** `[` *intExpression1*`,` *intExpression2* `]`

where the expressions evaluate to integers for the dimensions.

To assign the 8 in the table above, consider that it is in the second
row in normal counting, but we start array indices at 0, so there are
rows 0, 1, and 2, and the 8 has row index 1.
Again starting with index 0 for columns, the 8 is at index
1\. We can assign a value to that position with

In fact a two dimensional array just needs two indices that could mean
anything. For instance, it was just the standard convention,
calling the left index the row. They could have been switched everywhere, and
assume the notation `table[column, row]`:

int[,] table = new int[4, 3];
table[2, 1] = 8;

but we will *stick with* the original `[row, column]` model.

Data indexed by more than two integer indices can be stored in a higher
dimension array, with more indices between the square braces. We
will only consider two dimensional arrays in the examples here.

analogous to initializing one dimensional arrays is:

## Advanced topic: Array of Arrays

Since you can have an array of any type, it is also possible to have an
*array of arrays* (jagged arrays). The notational difference to a
multi-dimensional array is just that each index is enclosed in
separate square brackets, with no commas.

For example, you could create a table with shape like the initial example
in {ref}`2D-arrays`, less the last two elements to show the jagged array:

This takes somewhat more memory and is longer to
access than the multidimensional arrays. For most uses, when you want to
refer to a rectangular table of data, like above,
this new version has little to offer.

There are a couple of reasons why you might want this format.

First you may have functions that operate on one dimensional arrays,
and individual rows of `table2` are one dimensional arrays:

## Let a Helper Promise Exactly One Smaller Problem

A public method can accept a complete report while a private recursive helper accepts a suffix or range. The helper contract must name that smaller problem precisely. For a suffix starting at index i, the result might be the total of entries i through the end. The public caller starts with i zero; other starting indexes are an implementation detail rather than a burden placed on every client.

The base case is an empty suffix, not a special final value guessed from one example. Its sum is zero. For a nonempty suffix, combine the first available entry with the helper's result on the remaining suffix. The progress measure n-i decreases by one, which connects the contract to termination. The caller still needs an arithmetic-range policy: termination does not prove that a fixed-width sum cannot overflow.

For divide-and-conquer, represent a range as [lo, hi). Its length is hi-lo, and empty means lo equals hi. Splitting at lo+(hi-lo)/2 gives two adjacent half-open ranges. On five items, the lengths are two and three; neither item duplication nor equal lengths are required. What matters is complete, nonoverlapping coverage and strictly smaller children when recursion continues.

| Design question | What to state before recursing |
| --- | --- |
| What does the helper return? | A result for this suffix/range |
| When is the answer direct? | Empty/singleton or another explicit base |
| What becomes smaller? | Remaining length or another well-founded measure |
| How are child results combined? | An operation justified by the parent contract |

Guided contrast: finding a maximum needs results from both halves, while a binary-search comparison chooses only one remaining half. Both use interval splitting, but they do not have the same call tree or work recurrence. Predict child calls for one size-five input under each algorithm before comparing their costs.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Recursive Problem Solving ```

Basic recursive cases, base answers, and call/return tracing are taught in {doc}`Chapter 17 <../17_trees/1701_tree_structure>`. Review that section before this optional extension. Here you develop helper contracts, progress arguments, resource limits, and divide-and-conquer design.

```{index} Progress Measures
```

## Progress Measures
```{index} Progress Measures
A progress measure proves that recursion is moving in the right direction. The measure does not have to be a single number, but it must get closer to a base case.

The wrapper hides the helper index so clients cannot supply a negative or out-of-range start. Scan(index) promises whether the target occurs in the suffix [index,n). An empty suffix returns false; a matching first item returns true; otherwise the answer comes from the smaller suffix. The measure n−index decreases on every recursive call. Empty input needs no array access. Worst-case time and stack are Θ(n); a first-item match needs only one helper frame.

```{index} Recursion and Iteration
```

## Recursion and Iteration
```{index} Recursion and Iteration
Many recursive methods can be written with loops. Use recursion when the problem naturally breaks into smaller problems of the same shape, or when recursion makes the structure easier to see.

Both sums visit every item, taking Θ(n) time under the integer cost model. The recursive version retains Θ(n) active frames; an iterative sum retains Θ(1) auxiliary state. Recursion changes expression of control flow, not the amount of data that must be processed. Prefer the loop for long flat reports; recursion is particularly useful for balanced splits and nested structures.

```{index} Recursive Risks
```

## Recursive Risks
```{index} Recursive Risks

A recursive method with a missing base case or no progress can call itself forever until the program runs out of stack space. In C#, recursive calls are not something to use casually for huge linear loops.

Check input domain, direct base answer, and a well-founded progress measure before running recursive code. Do not intentionally trigger stack exhaustion in the browser. Tail-call elimination is not guaranteed for these C# methods. A finite domain and arithmetic range are separate from the proof of termination; validate both when designing the interface.

```{index} Exercise
```

## Exercise
```{index} Exercise
Recursively count positive expense adjustments in a suffix. Zero is not positive. State the helper postcondition and progress measure; test empty input.
```{index} Divide-and-Conquer Design ```

Divide-and-conquer algorithms solve a problem in three phases: divide the input into smaller parts, solve the smaller parts, and combine their results. Recursion is a natural implementation technique because each subproblem has the same shape as the original problem.

```{index} The Pattern
```

## The Pattern
```{index} The Pattern

A divide-and-conquer method usually follows this shape:

1. If the problem is small enough, solve it directly.
2. Divide the input into smaller pieces.
3. Recursively solve the pieces.
4. Combine the partial answers.

The helper promise is the maximum of the nonempty half-open range [start,end). The wrapper rejects empty input before recursion. For length>1, both child ranges are nonempty, smaller, disjoint, and together cover the parent, including odd lengths. Inductively correct child maxima combine to the parent maximum. The size measure end−start decreases. T(n)=T(floor(n/2))+T(ceil(n/2))+Θ(1), hence Θ(n) work and Θ(log n) stack. A loop also takes Θ(n) work with less stack: splitting alone does not make maximum selection faster.

```{index} Halving Strategies
```

## Halving Strategies
```{index} Halving Strategies
Some algorithms solve only one half after dividing. Binary search is the classic example: compare with the middle value, then search the half where the target could still be.

Precondition: input is sorted in ascending order and is not modified during the search. The result is any matching index, or −1 when absent; duplicates do not promise a first match. The candidate interval is [start,end). Sortedness justifies discarding the impossible side. Excluding middle from the right interval prevents repeating a one-item range. Each surviving range is smaller; an empty range stops recursion. Only one child is explored, giving T(n)=T(floor(n/2))+Θ(1) as a size model, Θ(log n) worst-case time/stack, and Θ(1) best-case time. Checking sortedness on every call would add linear work.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^2201_recursion-1]: Tail-call optimization is not something introductory C# programmers should rely on. Prefer clear loops for simple linear repetition when stack depth could become large.
[^2201_recursion-2]: A recursive method can have more than one base case. The important point is that every path of recursive calls eventually reaches one of them.

## Prove the Combining Step Before Hiding It in Recursion

Assume two input runs are already sorted under the same policy. To merge them, compare their first unread elements and choose the smaller. No later element in either run can be smaller than that run's first unread element, so the chosen value is safe as the next output. Recursion supplies sorted runs; it does not remove the need to justify this combining rule.

Merge [2, 5] with [1, 5, 7]. Choose 1 from the right, then 2 from the left. At the tie between the two 5 values, choosing the left one first preserves relative order when these runs came from adjacent parts of the original input. After one run is exhausted, copy the remaining suffix of the other; it is already sorted.

| Output so far | Left unread | Right unread |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [] | 2, 5 | 1, 5, 7 |
| [1] | 2, 5 | 5, 7 |
| [1, 2] | 5 | 5, 7 |
| [1, 2, 5-left] | Empty | 5-right, 7 |

The invariant combines ordering and preservation: output contains exactly the consumed input occurrences in sorted order, and its final element is no greater than the remaining candidates. Keeping only the ordering claim would not rule out accidentally duplicating one occurrence and losing another.

Range/buffer implementations add an indexing obligation. Source and destination ranges must refer to the intended segments; copying into the wrong offset can produce correct tiny whole-array results and fail on an interior range. Trace a merge whose lo is not zero, and include odd lengths. A reusable buffer can reduce allocation without changing the merge contract.

Guided verification: label equal invoice amounts with original IDs. Check that sorted order holds, every original ID occurs exactly once, and equal-key IDs retain their arrival order. Then compare a nonmutating sort that returns a fresh outer array with an in-place sort. Both may order values correctly, but only one satisfies a contract that preserves the caller's original array order.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

```{index} Combining Sorted Parts
```

## Combining Sorted Parts
```{index} Combining Sorted Parts
Merge sort depends on a combine step called **merge**. Given two sorted arrays, merge walks through both arrays and builds one sorted result.

Merge requires two inputs sorted under the same comparison, and returns a fresh sorted array containing every input occurrence. At the main loop head, k=i+j and result[0,k) is the stable sorted merge of the consumed prefixes. The next smallest unconsumed item must be at one of the two fronts. Choosing the left front on equality preserves original order. Once one side is exhausted, copy the other remainder without further comparisons. For total N>0, merging takes Θ(N) time/output space and at most N−1 key comparisons; empty sides can need zero comparisons but still require copying.

```{index} Merge Sort
```

## Merge Sort
```{index} Merge Sort
Merge sort divides the array into halves until each piece has zero or one item, then merges sorted pieces back together.

The copy-returning contract leaves the input unchanged and returns a fresh array even for zero or one item. Slices allocate new arrays, making this version easy to read but allocation-heavy. T(n)=T(floor(n/2))+T(ceil(n/2))+Θ(n), so time is Θ(n log n) for n≥2. Stack depth is Θ(log n). The next section replaces slices with index ranges and a reusable buffer; it also verifies stability and preservation. Comparisons are only one part of sorting cost: copying still happens when a side is exhausted.

```{index} Design Checklist
```

## Design Checklist
```{index} Design Checklist

When designing a divide-and-conquer algorithm, ask:

1. What is the smallest case I can solve directly?
2. How do I divide the input?
3. Do I solve one subproblem or multiple subproblems?
4. How do I combine the answers?
5. What recurrence describes the cost?

```{index} Exercise
```

## Exercise
```{index} Exercise
Merge two sorted invoice batches, including duplicates and an empty side. Verify the exact expected sequence, not just increasing order.
```{index} Merge Sort Lab ```

A finance team sorts invoices by amount while retaining the arrival order of equal amounts. Build correctness checks before comparing counts. Every code cell includes its own setup and implementation.

Download {download}`the complete stable merge-sort source and reference checks <../../demos/22_recursion_divide_conquer/StableSort.cs>` for a console project.

```{index} Trace Merge Fronts
```

## Trace Merge Fronts
```{index} Trace Merge Fronts
Track consumed indexes i and j and output index k. Equal keys take the left item first. Predict which side runs out, then trace both the comparison loop and the tail copies.

The invariant k=i+j and sorted consumed-prefix merge explains why no value disappears. The measure (left.Length−i)+(right.Length−j) decreases after every copy. Stability is relative to a comparison key; equal integer values cannot display record order, so use labeled invoices next.

```{index} Sort Ranges with One Buffer
```

## Sort Ranges with One Buffer
```{index} Sort Ranges with One Buffer

The public method clones the input once and allocates one reusable buffer. SortRange(start,end) sorts a half-open range. Sibling calls finish sequentially, then merge their sorted ranges into the matching buffer range and copy back. Counts reset at each Sort call.

Assume each recursive call correctly sorts its smaller range and preserves its items. The merge invariant establishes the same promise for the parent. Empty/singleton ranges return directly. Odd lengths are fully covered. The copied output and buffer use Θ(n) storage, and the stack adds Θ(log n); total auxiliary space is Θ(n). Across all levels there are Θ(n log n) writes, but cumulative writes are not peak memory. The original slice version also allocates across levels; separate total allocation volume from peak live storage.

```{index} Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices
```

## Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices
```{index} Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices

A stable sort preserves arrival order among equal amounts. Compare only the amount, and track identity separately. A consistent comparison must define an ordering; subtracting integer keys can overflow, so use CompareTo.

Changing the merge comparison from ≤0 to <0 would let equal right items overtake equal left items. Stability matters when reports preserve earlier arrival order or apply successive sorts. It is a property of the algorithm and comparison policy, not merely of sorted numeric output.

```{index} Check Order, Preservation, and Copying
```

## Check Order, Preservation, and Copying
```{index} Check Order, Preservation, and Copying

Sortedness alone is insufficient: returning an empty array is sorted but loses every invoice. Compare against an independent sorted reference, check input preservation and array identity, and include empty, singleton, odd, duplicate, reverse, negative, and extreme cases.

```{index} Compare Measured Operations
```

## Compare Measured Operations
```{index} Compare Measured Operations

Count actual key comparisons and element writes. The asymptotic expression n log₂ n is a growth model, not an exact comparison count. Different orders can exhaust one merge side earlier. Buffer copy-back contributes writes even after comparisons stop.

For powers of two, this implementation performs exactly 2n log₂ n counted writes: one buffer write and one copy-back write per item per internal level. Clone and buffer allocation are setup and are excluded from that counter, but included in the algorithm’s overall cost. Recursion has 2n−1 calls for nonempty input. Time remains Θ(n log n); these are deterministic operation counts, not timings.

```{index} Exercise
```

## Practice: Verify Merge Results
```{index} Exercise
Sort labeled invoices by amount in descending order while preserving arrival order for ties. Test int.MinValue and int.MaxValue safely. Reverse the comparison operands; do not subtract keys.

# Recursion and Divide-and-Conquer A recursive call is useful when a smaller problem has a precise contract and makes progress toward a base case. This chapter connects separate call frames and returned values to divide-and-conquer design, then develops stable merge sort. You will verify splitting, occurrence preservation, tie policies, and auxiliary storage as well as sorted output. - **Base case**: The condition that stops recursion with a direct answer. - **Recursive case**: The part of the method that calls itself on a smaller input. - **Progress measure**: A quantity that moves toward the base case on every recursive call. - **Call stack**: The runtime structure that tracks active method calls and their local variables. - **Divide-and-conquer**: A design pattern that divides a problem, solves subproblems, and combines results.

Glossary

| # | Term | Explanation |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Recursion | A technique where a method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller input. |
| 2 | Base case | A directly solved case that stops recursive calls. |
| 3 | Recursive case | The branch that makes one or more recursive calls. |
| 4 | Progress measure | A value, such as `n` or a range length, that gets closer to the base case with each call. |
| 5 | Call stack | The runtime stack of active method calls. |
| 6 | Stack frame | One active method call and its local state on the call stack. |
| 7 | Divide-and-conquer | An algorithm design pattern that splits a problem into subproblems, solves them, and combines the answers. |
| 8 | Subproblem | A smaller version of the original problem. |
| 9 | Combine step | The step that merges subproblem results into a final answer. |
| 10 | Merge | The process of combining two sorted sequences into one sorted sequence. |
| 11 | Merge sort | A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that recursively sorts halves and merges them. |
| 12 | Half-open range | A range [start,end) including start but excluding end. |
| 13 | Helper contract | The promise made by a recursive subproblem method. |
| 14 | Inductive reasoning | A direct base result plus a correct combination of smaller correct results. |
| 15 | Stable sort | A sort preserving arrival order among equal comparison keys. |
| 16 | Occurrence preservation | Keeping every input item with its original multiplicity. |
| 17 | Shared merge buffer | A reusable temporary array used by successive merges. |
| 18 | Shallow array copy | A new array whose element references or values are copied without cloning referenced objects. |
| 19 | Peak active frames | Maximum calls simultaneously retained on the stack, including the base frame here. |

(preface)=

# Preface

This book teaches you to think like a computer scientist while you write real C# programs. It assumes no programming experience. The first course develops the skills to build a small multi-class information system that stores its data in a database. Further study introduces data structures and the algorithmic foundations needed to choose and use them. An optional algorithms sequence develops deeper analysis and problem-solving techniques.

The book is about computer science and information technology, not only C# syntax. Each chapter pairs a programming skill with the idea behind it: why a program is split into methods, why a dictionary finds a key faster than a list, why one algorithm finishes in a second while another would run for years. The examples come from business and management settings such as sales, inventory, payroll, scheduling, and delivery routes, so the problems look like the ones organizations actually solve with software.

The code cells in this book run as written. Change a value, run the cell again, and see what happens; that habit is how programming is learned.

```{index} AI and programming
```

## Why Coding When AI Writes Code

AI assistants now generate working code from a short description. That makes the skills in this book more important, not less. Someone still has to state precisely what a program should do, decides whether the code an assistant produces is correct, work with the agents to make sure the development is in the right direction, and judge which tradeoffs make better sense. 

Those are the skills this book practices. You will trace method calls by hand (Chapter 5), test and debug code systematically (Chapter 6), state preconditions and loop invariants, and compare operation costs using Big-O notation (Chapter 13), with deeper analysis in Chapter 21. A developer who can do these things uses AI as a fast assistant. A developer who cannot is left trusting output they are unable to check.

```{index} book organization; instructors
```

## How the Book Is Organized

The book has seven parts. Parts I-III develop an applied programming foundation. Parts IV-V supply the data-structures foundation, and Parts VI-VII offer selectable algorithm analysis, design, and optimization.

| Part | Chapters | Role in the sequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I. Fundamentals | 1-6 | Introduce computing concepts and C# programs, then develop decisions, iteration, methods, testing, and responsible professional practice. |
| II. Data and I/O | 7-9 | Organize records in arrays and collections, and read, write, and process files and text. |
| III. Object-Oriented Programming | 10-12 | Model application data and behavior with classes, apply object-oriented principles, and organize the earlier data workflows into reusable components. |
| IV. Data Abstraction and Linear Structures | 13-16 | Define ADTs, introduce practical cost analysis, implement linear structures, and compare basic searching and sorting. |
| V. Trees, Hashing, and Graphs | 17-20 | Introduce recursion with trees, then study heaps, hashing, and graph traversal. |
| VI. Algorithm Analysis and Design | 21-23 | Develop deeper cost/correctness reasoning, recursive design, divide and conquer, and advanced searching and sorting. |
| VII. Optimization and Computational Limits | 24-26 | Explore greedy methods, dynamic programming, backtracking, advanced graph/string applications, and computational limits. |

The {doc}`Contents <contents>` lists the chapters and sections, and {doc}`Chapter Topics <chapter_topics>` provides a more detailed overview. The appendices supply resources, command-line and GitHub guidance, the group project, and instructor-facing curriculum alignment.

```{index} course pathways; College of Business
```

## Course Pathways

**Programming and Information Systems Foundations (Chapters 1-12)** can serve as a first-semester course. Students progress from small console programs to methods, collections, files, classes, and object-oriented design. Integration, testing, documentation, and a project demonstration bring these skills together.

**Data Structures and Algorithms Foundations (Parts IV-V, Chapters 13-20)** can serve as a second course for students who already have the first course's programming foundation. Parts IV-V develop representation choices and their algorithmic foundations. Parts VI-VII (Chapters 21-26) provide optional deeper analysis and design. An instructor using this portion independently should establish equivalent preparation in methods, collections, classes, and interfaces.

**CS1 can use Parts I-III; CS2 can use Parts IV-V with selected Parts VI-VII chapters.** Chapters 1-12 provide the applied foundation, and instructors select Parts IV-V depth to fit their course goals. Parts IV-V include basic Big-O, linear and binary search, library sorting, recursion for tree operations, and breadth-first and depth-first graph traversal. Students can study these foundations without taking Parts VI-VII. Instructors may use the optional algorithms chapters for a technical specialization or further study.

A chapter is a weekly organizing unit, with roughly 100-120 minutes of planned lecture and additional practice. Course schedules also need time for review, assessment, and project integration; instructors can adjust the depth and pace rather than assign every topic in the volume.

The {ref}`Curriculum Alignment appendix <cs2023_alignment>` documents the book's contributions to both Information Systems (IS2020) and Computer Science (CS2023) curriculum guidance. The mappings help instructors identify relevant material and coverage boundaries; neither represents complete degree-program coverage.

```{index} chapter structure
```

## How Each Chapter Works

Each chapter is one week of work. A chapter opens with a landing page that lists its sections, followed by content sections, usually three, each sized for one class meeting. The first section introduces the chapter's main ideas, and the later sections each take one focused topic. Every section includes code you can run and modify.

The assignments follow the content:

- **Preview**: a short multiple-choice quiz on the chapter's key ideas, taken before or early in the week.
- **Lab**: connected coding practice on one theme, where each step builds on the previous one.
- **Homework**: true/false questions and coding problems that reinforce the chapter after class.
- **Project** (some chapters): a deliverable built in VS Code and submitted through GitHub, connecting the chapter to a larger application.

To get the most out of a chapter, read a section before class, run every example, then change it: use different input, break it on purpose, and read the error message. The labs and homework assume you have done this.

```{index} C#; why C#
```

## Why C\#

C# is a general-purpose, statically typed language at the center of Microsoft's open-source, cross-platform .NET platform. It is a good first language for this book for four reasons:

- **Types are visible.** Every variable has a declared type that the compiler checks before the program runs. Beginners see how data is represented, and many mistakes are caught as compile errors instead of surprising results.
- **It is used where business software is built.** C# and .NET power enterprise web services, internal business applications, cloud back ends, and database-driven systems, the same kind of information systems this book builds toward.
- **It is free and runs everywhere.** The .NET SDK and VS Code run on Windows, macOS, and Linux, so the tools you install in Chapter 1 are the tools professionals use.
- **The ideas transfer.** Classes, interfaces, generics, collections, and exceptions in C# map closely to Java, TypeScript, and other modern languages. The data structures and algorithms in Parts IV-VII apply in any language.

C# is widely used beyond business systems: the Unity game engine, ASP.NET web applications, and desktop and mobile apps are written in it. C# also holds a steady place among the most used languages. ```

```

## Acknowledgments

This book began from *Introduction to Computer Science in C#* by Andrew N. Harrington and George Thiruvathukal[^harrington_thiruvathukal], an open textbook that has served students at Loyola University Chicago and elsewhere for many years. *Computer Science in C#* reorganizes and extends that foundation with a week-by-week structure, runnable examples, business and management applications, and a second semester of data structures and algorithms.

```

[^stack-overflow-survey]: Stack Overflow (2025). Stack Overflow Annual Developer Survey. https://survey.stackoverflow.co/

Flexible Course Adoption

Parts I-III (Chapters 1-12) form a complete CS1 route. Parts IV-V (Chapters 13-20) supply the CS2 data-structures foundation. Parts VI-VII (Chapters 21-26) provide selectable algorithmic depth according to course goals and available time. The book supports COB, IST, IT, IS, and LIS programs as well as other programming-foundations courses; a standalone CS1 course needs no commitment to a second semester.

# Iterators

Every type in this chapter has been an ADT you interact with through explicit operations: `Push`, `Pop`, `Get`, `Set`. `foreach` is different — it is a loop that lets a *type* decide what "give me the next element" means, without the caller ever touching an index or a key. This section covers how that contract works, and how to implement it for your own types.

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

```{index} IEnumerable; IEnumerator
```

```{index} Why foreach Works
```

## Why foreach Works

```{index} Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One
```

```{index} Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One
```

## Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One

A collection knows where its elements are stored. A client often needs only to visit those elements in the promised order. Enumeration provides a boundary between those responsibilities. Foreach asks for an enumeration protocol rather than directly reading private array slots or node links.

For a simple countable sequence 2, 4, 6, imagine an enumerator positioned before the first value. A successful MoveNext advances to the next value and permits reading Current. After the final value, MoveNext reports false. The client does not invent an extra zero value merely because iteration has ended. This success/result separation resembles the Try operations from earlier collection lessons.

| Request | Outcome | Current value to consume |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First MoveNext | true | 2 |
| Second MoveNext | true | 4 |
| Third MoveNext | true | 6 |
| Fourth MoveNext | false | No next element |

An IEnumerable<T> describes something that can provide enumeration. An IEnumerator<T> represents progress through one enumeration. They are not interchangeable names for a collection. Multiple enumeration requests can have separate progress states, and a producer may compute elements instead of keeping all of them in a list.

```{index} A Yield Point Suspends Rather than Finishes the Sequence
```

```{index} A Yield Point Suspends Rather than Finishes the Sequence
```

## A Yield Point Suspends Rather than Finishes the Sequence

The pattern `IEnumerable<T> Produce(...) { ... yield return value; ... }` defines an iterator. Yielding supplies one element and suspends that enumeration's progress until the consumer requests another. An ordinary return from a value-returning method finishes that call; yield return participates in a sequence of resumptions. Explain this distinction before treating yield as abbreviated list construction.

Laziness changes when work and failures occur. Obtaining an enumerable need not run every statement that will produce its values. If the consumer stops after two elements, later elements may never be computed. An expensive calculation inside an iterator is not paid simply because an enumerable variable has been declared, but repeated enumerations may repeat that work. Do not promise caching unless the implementation explicitly provides it.

The producer also needs a mutation policy. An enumeration over shared mutable storage can be affected by changes made after the enumerable is obtained. Library collections may detect invalid mutation during enumeration; custom types must state their own behavior. Returning IEnumerable<T> does not automatically create a snapshot or make private storage immutable.

Guided prediction: an iterator announces each produced number and yields 2, 4, 6. A caller breaks after consuming 4. Which production announcements should appear? Then run a second enumeration and ask whether it starts with a fresh progress state. Use the existing runnable iterator examples to check your prediction and distinguish fresh enumeration from continuing one enumerator.

```{index} yield return
```

```{index} Writing an Iterator with yield return
```

## Writing an Iterator with yield return

Implementing `IEnumerator<T>` by hand — tracking a position field, writing `MoveNext()` and `Current` yourself — is tedious for something as simple as "count from one number to another." The `yield return` statement lets the compiler generate that machinery for you. A method that contains `yield return` becomes an iterator: each call to `yield return` produces one element and pauses; the method resumes from that point the next time an element is requested.

Nothing about `EvenNumbers` mentions `IEnumerator`, `MoveNext`, or `Current` — the compiler builds a hidden class that implements all of it. The method's return type is `IEnumerable<int>`, and the body describes *what to produce*, not *how to track position*.

```{index} IEnumerable; custom implementation
```

```{index} Making Your Own Type foreach-able
```

## Making Your Own Type foreach-able

A standalone iterator *method* is useful, but sometimes the thing you want to iterate is a type you have already defined — an ADT you built, not a built-in collection. To make `foreach` work directly on an instance of your type, implement `IEnumerable<T>` and put a `yield return` inside `GetEnumerator()`:

`IEnumerable<T>` requires the generic `GetEnumerator()`. The second, non-generic `IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` line is boilerplate C# requires because `IEnumerable<T>` itself extends the older, non-generic `IEnumerable` — it just forwards to the generic version above it. Once both are present, `NumberRange` works with `foreach`, LINQ, and any other API that accepts `IEnumerable<T>`, exactly like `List<T>` does.

```{index} iterator; lazy evaluation
```

```{index} Iterators Are Lazy
```

## Iterators Are Lazy

An iterator method does not run its body when you call it — it runs one step at a time, only as far as the caller actually asks for elements. Calling `EvenNumbers(1, 1000000)` returns instantly; the loop body only executes as `foreach` requests each next value. This matters for two reasons: an iterator can describe an infinite or unbounded sequence without ever running forever, and a `foreach` that stops early (with `break`) never computes the elements it never asked for.

```{index} Practice
```

## Practice

1. Write an iterator method `static IEnumerable<int> CountDown(int from)` that yields `from, from - 1, ..., 1`.
2. Write a class `Pair<T>` holding two values of type `T`, implementing `IEnumerable<T>` so that `foreach` over a `Pair<T>` yields both values in order.
3. Explain, in terms of the `IEnumerable<T>` / `IEnumerator<T>` contract from earlier in this section, why a type can be `foreach`-able without being indexable — that is, without supporting `range[i]`.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```

# Representations and Costs

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

Once an ADT contract is clear, the next question is representation: how should the data be stored so the required operations are correct and efficient?

```{index} One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work
```

```{index} One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work
```

## One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work

Use the undo contract from the preceding lesson. An array representation might keep active entries in positions zero through Count minus one. A linked representation might keep the newest entry at the head. The same Push/Pop history can be correct in both, yet their storage and work differ. To compare them fairly, hold the abstract behavior fixed and change only the representation.

For the array, Count and capacity answer different questions. Count describes active entries; capacity describes available slots in the allocated backing storage. A push with unused capacity writes one entry and increases Count. A push into full storage may allocate a larger array, copy active entries, and then append. Calling both pushes constant work ignores the copying performed by the growth case.

For a linked representation, a push can create one node whose next reference identifies the old head. Updating the head then makes the new node first. A pop can advance head to its next node. This avoids an array-wide growth copy, but node allocation and extra references are still real costs. Neither representation is universally better merely because one operation has a simple asymptotic label.

| Representation question | Array-backed history | Linked history |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How are active values located? | Used prefix of slots | Nodes reachable from head |
| What marks empty? | Count equals zero | No head node, with matching Count |
| What may make a push expensive? | Growth and copying | Allocation and runtime costs |
| What must stay hidden? | Unused capacity | Internal node links |

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

```{index} Define What You Count
```

```{index} Define What You Count
```

## Define What You Count

If the input size is the number n of active entries, counting element copies explains an array growth. Counting only calls to Push hides the difference among calls. Big-O summarizes a bound as n grows; it does not supply the cost model for you. State whether the analysis counts comparisons, copies, reference updates, or another operation.

An amortized append claim concerns a whole sequence of operations, including occasional expensive growth. It is not a claim that every individual append is cheap, and it is not an average over randomly selected inputs. Likewise, constant auxiliary storage describes additional working memory under a model; it does not mean the data structure itself occupies no memory.

Guided comparison: an array with Count three and capacity four receives two pushes. Explain why the first can use a free slot and the second may require growth. Draw the abstract history after both calls, then draw the different physical storage states. Keeping those drawings separate prevents a copied backing array from being mistaken for a changed ADT result.

```{index} representation; data structure
```
```{index} representation independence
```

```{index} One Contract, Multiple Representations
```

## One Contract, Multiple Representations

The same stack ADT can be represented in more than one way:

| Representation | Main idea |
| --- | --- |
| Array-backed stack | Store items in contiguous slots and track the top index. |
| List-backed stack | Delegate storage growth to `List<T>`. |
| Linked-node stack | Store each item in a node that references the next node. |

If all three preserve the same contract, client code can use them through the same interface. This is **representation independence**.

```{index} array-backed stack
```

```{index} Array-Backed Stack
```

## Array-Backed Stack

An array-backed stack stores items from left to right. The next available index is also the current count.

```text
items: [A] [B] [C] [ ] [ ]
count: 3
top:   C
```

Pushing writes into `items[count]`, then increments `count`. Popping decrements `count`, reads the value, and clears the slot.

```{index} linked nodes
```
```{index} reference; linked structure
```

```{index} Linked Nodes and References
```

## Linked Nodes and References

A linked representation stores each item in a small object called a node. Each node holds a value and a reference to the next node.

```text
top -> [C | next] -> [B | next] -> [A | null]
```

The variable `top` does not contain the whole stack. It contains a reference to the first node. Following references reveals the rest of the structure.

```{index} Counting Work and Big-O
```

## Counting Work and Big-O

```{index} Big O; input size; auxiliary space
```

Let `n` be the number of records. Count a representative operation before comparing implementations. **Big-O** describes an upper bound on how work grows with input size, ignoring fixed factors for sufficiently large inputs. It is not an elapsed time or automatically a worst-case claim.

| Bound | Example | Effect of doubling input |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | Reading one array slot | Bounded work independent of size. |
| O(log n) | Repeatedly halving a search interval | About one extra halving. |
| O(n) | Scanning all records | About twice the work. |
| O(n log n) | A typical comparison sort | Slightly more than twice the work. |
| O(n²) | Comparing every pair | About four times the work. |

These are useful upper bounds; a linear scan is also O(n²), but O(n) is more informative. A **tight bound**, written Θ, describes the actual growth order under the stated model. Later chapters use Θ when both upper and lower growth bounds are known.

This example counts exactly `n` additions. Array access and fixed-width arithmetic are treated as constant-cost operations. A comparison of long strings can depend on string length.

Specify the case: a search may stop at the first record or inspect all `n`. **Amortized cost** averages over a sequence of operations: geometric array growth permits O(1) amortized append even though a resizing append takes O(n). This does not make every append constant-time. **Auxiliary space** counts extra storage beyond the input; a running total takes O(1), while an additional copy takes O(n). Chapter 21 develops formal bounds and richer cost models.

Before running, predict the addition counts for sizes zero, one, four, and eight. Then explain why reading only `expenses[0]` has a different growth bound and needs a nonempty-input precondition.

```{index} operation cost
```
```{index} Big O; collection operations
```

```{index} Operation Costs
```

## Operation Costs

A data structure is not just correct or incorrect. It also has costs.

| Operation | Array/List-backed stack | Linked-node stack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Push` | Usually O(1); occasional resize costs O(n) | O(1) |
| `Pop` | O(1) | O(1) |
| `Peek` | O(1) | O(1) |
| Random access by index | O(1), if exposed | O(n) |
| Extra memory per item | low | one extra reference per node |

The best representation depends on the workload. If a program mostly pushes and pops at one end, either representation can work. If it needs fast index access, linked nodes are the wrong fit.

```{index} Practice
```

## Practice

1. Draw the linked-node diagram after pushing `"red"`, `"blue"`, and `"green"` onto a stack.
2. Explain why resizing an array-backed stack is occasional O(n), even though most pushes are O(1).
3. Choose a representation for an undo history and justify it using operation costs.

```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

A representation is the hidden storage strategy behind an ADT contract. Arrays, lists, and linked nodes make different tradeoffs in speed, memory use, and flexibility. Data-structure design is the art of matching those tradeoffs to the operations a program performs most often.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```
[^1302_representations_costs-1]: Big-O compares growth under an explicit cost model. Chapter 21 extends these foundations with formal bounds, correctness arguments, and recurrences.

[^development-reading]: Further reading: [OpenDSA, Lists: Chapter Introduction](https://opendsa.org/OpenDSA/Books/Catalog/html/ListIntro.html). The worked business scenarios and guided reasoning here are original teaching examples.

# ADT Contracts

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

An **abstract data type** starts with behavior. Before deciding whether data should be stored in an array, linked nodes, or a hash table, we decide what operations the type promises to support.

```{index} Describe the Observable History First
```

```{index} Describe the Observable History First
```

## Describe the Observable History First

An undo history is not defined by an array or a linked node. It is defined by what a client can observe after a sequence of operations. If the client records A, records B, and then undoes once, it expects B to be removed before A. An implementation can store those entries in different ways while preserving that behavior. This separates the abstract data type, the behavioral contract, from the data structure used to realize it.

Write the history on paper before writing a class. For each operation, record the result, the resulting abstract contents, and the empty/failure policy. If the contract says an unsuccessful TryPop leaves state unchanged, returning false after already decrementing Count violates the contract even if later tests happen to restore the count.

| Operation | Result | Abstract history, oldest to newest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Empty | [] |
| Push A | Recorded | [A] |
| Push B | Recorded | [A, B] |
| TryPop | Success, B | [A] |
| TryPop | Success, A | [] |
| TryPop | Failure | [] |

The empty failure is part of the behavior, not an implementation detail to settle later. A different ADT might throw on an empty Pop. Both can be coherent contracts, but a client written for one cannot assume the other. Also specify whether null entries, duplicates, or a fixed capacity are allowed. These policies determine which tests should succeed and what failure must preserve.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

```{index} Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge
```

```{index} Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge
```

## Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge

A C# interface can express operation names and types, for example a success-returning method with an out result. It cannot by itself express every ordering rule or state invariant. Two classes can compile against the same interface and still behave differently. Tests and explanations connect the syntax to the promised history.

The client should not need to know the backing array's capacity or the head node's field name. If a capacity change affects returned values or exposes unused slots, representation details have leaked through the abstraction. Conversely, the implementer must know enough about storage to maintain its invariants. Abstraction assigns different responsibilities to the two roles; it does not mean that implementation details are unimportant.

Guided exercise: keep the interface unchanged but change removal to return A before B. Identify the first row at which this behavior differs from the specified history. Then explain why a test that checks only Count would miss the defect. Extend the history with a failed removal followed by a new push; this checks whether failure left the structure reusable.

```{dropdown} Contract checkpoint
The first successful removal must return B. A queue-like implementation could keep the right counts while returning the wrong element. Checking returned values, order, state after failure, and later reuse tests more of the contract than checking size alone.
```

```{index} abstract data type
```
```{index} contract; data structure
```

```{index} What an ADT Specifies
```

## What an ADT Specifies

An ADT describes a set of values and the operations allowed on those values. It does **not** require one particular internal representation.

For a stack, the contract might say:

| Operation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Push(item)` | Add an item to the top. |
| `Pop()` | Remove and return the top item. |
| `Peek()` | Return the top item without removing it. |
| `Count` | Report how many items are stored. |

This contract says nothing about arrays or linked lists. That separation is the point: client code should depend on the behavior it needs, not on accidental implementation details.

```{index} interface; ADT
```

```{index} Interfaces as Contracts
```

## Interfaces as Contracts
In C#, an `interface` is a natural way to write an ADT contract. It names the operations but leaves the storage strategy to a class.

```{index} client code
```

```{index} Client Code Depends on Behavior
```

## Client Code Depends on Behavior

**Client code** is code that uses a type. If client code only needs stack behavior, it should not care whether the stack is backed by a `List<T>`, an array, or linked nodes.

That means this is a better variable type for many methods:

```csharp
static void UndoLastAction(IStack<string> actions)
```

than this:

```csharp
static void UndoLastAction(ListStack<string> actions)
```

The first version accepts any stack implementation that satisfies the contract.

```{index} invariant
```

```{index} Contracts Include Rules
```

## Contracts Include Rules

A contract includes more than method names. It also includes rules:

- `Pop` removes the same item that `Peek` would return.
- `Count` increases after `Push` and decreases after `Pop`.
- `Pop` and `Peek` on an empty stack are errors.

A rule that must remain true for the object to be valid is called an **invariant**. Data-structure code often exists to preserve invariants while operations run quickly.

```{index} Practice
```

## Practice

1. Write a contract for a queue ADT using operation names and meanings.
2. Name one invariant a queue implementation must preserve.
3. Explain why a method parameter typed as `IStack<string>` is more flexible than one typed as `ListStack<string>`.

```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

An ADT names behavior. An interface can express that behavior in C#. Implementations provide storage and algorithms behind the contract. This separation lets programs change representation without changing every caller.

# Generics for Reusable ADTs

You have been using generics since Chapter 8: `List<T>` and `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`. In an ADT, generics let one contract and one implementation work with many element types while preserving compile-time type checking.

```{contents}
:local:

```

```{index} Why Generics Exist
```

## Why Generics Exist

```{index} Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types
```

```{index} Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types
```

## Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types

An undo history of product codes and a history of numeric adjustments can follow the same push/pop rules. Writing two unrelated implementations repeats the same invariant and creates two places to repair a defect. A generic type makes the element type a parameter while leaving the behavioral algorithm shared.

Read `History<T>` as a type definition with an element-type placeholder. Read `History<string>` as one constructed type whose element operations must accept strings. The placeholder is not a variable containing an element and is not a request to decide the type afresh on every assignment. A History<int> and a History<string> are different constructed types even though their operation names are the same.

The general class pattern is `class Container<T> { /* members that use T */ }`. A generic method has its own type parameter list, as in `static T Identity<T>(T value)`. These are declaration patterns, not complete programs. In concrete use the compiler checks compatible argument/result types. That lets a bad element insertion be rejected before a client discovers an incompatible value during a later cast.

```{index} State Which Operations the Generic Code Needs
```

```{index} State Which Operations the Generic Code Needs
```

## State Which Operations the Generic Code Needs

An unconstrained T supports being stored, passed and returned. It does not promise a Price property or a meaningful greater-than operation. If the algorithm needs ordering, supply an ordering policy or an appropriate constraint. If it needs key identity, supply an equality/hash policy with its consistency requirements. Ordering and equality are related concepts but different contracts.

| Algorithm purpose | Information needed beyond storage |
| --- | --- |
| Return the most recently stored item | No ordering comparison |
| Sort values for a report | A consistent ordering policy |
| Find a key in a hash table | Equality and compatible hashing |
| Call an element-specific capability | An explicit capability constraint |

A comparer can say that two invoices have equal totals even when they are distinct invoices. A key-equality policy might instead use invoice ID. Choosing a generic collection does not choose those business meanings automatically. Avoid solving a missing requirement by converting every value to text and comparing that text; it can change numeric order and lose distinctions.

Guided design: create a generic history interface for values that never need to be compared. Would requiring all element types to implement an ordering interface help? It would unnecessarily reject useful element types. Add constraints because an operation needs them, not because generics seem advanced. The short lambda/query forms later in this lesson are a bridge for reading policy arguments; the fundamental generic contract does not depend on mastering LINQ.

## Generic Classes

## Type Constraints

Use `where T : ...` to restrict what types `T` can be. Constraints are useful when an ADT operation needs a capability that not every type has.

| Constraint | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `where T : class` | T must be a reference type |
| `where T : struct` | T must be a value type |
| `where T : new()` | T must have a parameterless constructor |
| `where T : ISomeInterface` | T must implement the interface |
| `where T : BaseClass` | T must inherit from `BaseClass` |

```{index} generic interface
```

```{index} Generic Interfaces

## Generic Interfaces

```{index} Ordering and Equality Are Different Contracts
```

## Ordering and Equality Are Different Contracts

```{index} Ordering and Equality Are Different Contracts
```

An ordering comparer answers before, tied, or after with a negative value, zero, or a positive value. An equality comparer answers whether two values identify the same key. A price tie does not make two products the same product. Supply the same ordering policy to sorting and binary search; supply matching Equals and GetHashCode policies to hash collections. Equal keys must have equal hash codes, but unequal keys can collide. Never change a stored key in a way that changes its equality or hash value.

The named AmountComparer implements IComparer<Invoice>. Comparing Amount uses decimal.CompareTo, which avoids arithmetic subtraction and conversion. A comparer must be consistent and transitive. Array.Sort does not promise arrival order for tied values. A stable sorting algorithm preserves that order; Chapter 16 makes the distinction visible.

```{index} Reading Short Expressions and Queries
```

## Reading Short Expressions and Queries

```{index} Reading Short Expressions and Queries
```

Later collection examples sometimes use compact C# forms. The expression x => x > 0 is a lambda: a function receiving x and returning the comparison result. A library method can call that function for each value. Where filters values, Select transforms them, OrderBy orders them, and ToArray materializes a separate array. These LINQ extension methods require using System.Linq. Prefer an explicit loop when it makes the algorithm or mutation clearer. Query pipelines can defer work until enumeration; ToArray executes the pipeline now.

An expression-bodied member such as public int Count => items.Count; is shorthand for a getter returning that expression. A target-typed new() uses the declared variable type, so List<int> values = new(); constructs a List<int>. Neither abbreviation changes the data-structure contract. Named classes and explicit constructors remain useful while learning a new model.

(abstract-data-types)= # Abstract Data Types A client needs to know what a collection promises before it needs to know where the values live. This chapter connects abstract data type contracts to representations, invariants, generics, iteration, and operation costs. # Choosing and Coordinating Collections
