:local:
:depth: 2
```

```{index} Coordinate Indexes with One Consistency Story
```

```{index} Coordinate Indexes with One Consistency Story
```

## Coordinate Indexes with One Consistency Story

A dispatch system wants quick lookup by ticket ID and repeated service by priority. One collection may not efficiently supply both operations under the required policies. A dictionary can locate the current ticket by ID while a priority queue selects service candidates. Using two indexes introduces an obligation: their views must not cause cancelled or superseded work to be served.

One design permits stale queue entries and checks them when removed. The dictionary holds authoritative current state. A queue candidate is served only if its ID still exists and its version matches the current ticket. Cancellation removes or marks the authoritative record; old queue entries can be skipped later. Versioning matters when the same ID can be updated: mere presence is not proof that the old priority entry still describes the current work.

| Event | Authoritative lookup | Old queue entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Register ticket | Present with current version | Eligible when selected |
| Cancel ticket | Absent or explicitly cancelled | Skip |
| Change priority/version | Updated current version | Skip if its version is stale |

The alternative is to remove/update queue entries eagerly, which needs suitable index support and its own maintenance rules. Compare complete workflows rather than declaring either approach universally faster. Lazy cleanup simplifies some updates but can retain stale storage and make later removals perform extra work.

Guided trace: register ticket A, cancel A, register a new version of A, then remove an old queue candidate. Explain why matching only the ID can serve the wrong version. Extend the trace with a failed lookup and check that it changes neither index. The existing cancellation example is an entry point to this consistency reasoning, not a guarantee that every multi-index update is automatically transactional.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

A service application may need exact lookup, uniqueness checks, ordered reports, and priority dispatch at the same time. Name each operation before choosing a representation. Multiple indexes are useful only if updates preserve a clear agreement between them.

```{index} Match the Structure to the Workload
```

## Match the Structure to the Workload
```{index} workload; data-structure choice

The same service desk has several access needs. Use a priority queue for the next urgent ticket, a dictionary for its owner, and a set for uniqueness or closed-ticket membership. A tree supports ordered keys and range queries. Each structure preserves a different relationship; the application must keep shared IDs consistent.

| Need | Structure | Cost under stated assumptions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Select next urgency | Heap priority queue | O(log n) repair; backing-array growth can make one enqueue O(n). |
| Find owner by ID | Hash dictionary | Expected O(1) with well-distributed hashing and bounded load; worst-case O(n). |
| Reject duplicate ID | Hash set or dictionary | Expected O(1) under the same assumptions. |
| Ordered interval report | Balanced search tree | O(log n + k) for k results; the Chapter 16 unbalanced tree depends on actual height. |
| Process by arrival | FIFO queue | Constant-time endpoints in the linked representation. |

These bounds assume fixed-cost comparison and hashing. They describe operations, not measured milliseconds. A tiny list can still be a practical choice when there are few records and little repeated lookup.

Download {download}`the complete heap and chained-map source with verification <../../demos/19_hash_collections/HeapHashStructures.cs>` to use in a console project.

```{index} Count Work Before Timing
```

## Count Work Before Timing
```{index} hashing; operation count; performance measurement

One stopwatch measurement includes runtime warm-up, scheduling noise, and timer granularity. It cannot establish a complexity bound. First compare the amount of relevant work. In the controlled example below, the list must inspect every key for an absent lookup, while an explicitly constructed chain table inspects only the selected bucket.

The small hash function deliberately maps nonnegative integer IDs by remainder. This is a reproducible placement experiment, not instrumentation of .NET Dictionary.

The absent lookup uses 1000 comparisons in the list and 10 in the selected chain. With a constant hash function, all keys would occupy one chain and the lookup would again require 1000 comparisons. Collision distribution explains the difference.

A benchmark should separate construction from the operation being studied, repeat lookups over representative hit/miss keys, warm up the runtime, report variation, and include realistic key-hashing costs. Those measurements complement the analysis; they do not turn expected constant-time hashing into a worst-case guarantee. Chapter 19 develops analysis and measurement further.

```{index} Dispatch from Two Consistent Indexes
```

## Dispatch from Two Consistent Indexes
```{index} priority queue; dictionary; consistency

The service desk keeps active records in a dictionary and pending IDs in a priority queue. A simple cancellation policy removes the active record while leaving its old queue entry in place. On dequeue, skip IDs no longer active. This is **lazy deletion**: defer physical cleanup until an obsolete entry reaches the front.

This example allows each ID to be registered once during the batch. If an ID can be reused or reprioritized, an old entry may still refer to an active ID. Use a generation/version field and verify it on dequeue, or implement an indexed heap with explicit updates. Presence alone would then be insufficient.

The cancelled urgent ticket is skipped, then T-100 and T-102 are served in their arrival order. Immediately after cancellation, the dictionary has two entries but the queue still has three. Equal Counts are not the invariant. Every active record has one live pending entry, while pending may also contain inactive IDs.

Skipping one stale entry costs one heap removal. Across a batch, each enqueued entry is removed at most once, but a single request for the next active ticket may skip many cancelled entries. Cancellation also leaves queue storage occupied until cleanup. Analyze both the whole workload and an individual call; do not promise that lazy deletion makes every dispatch O(log n).

```{index} Explain the Selection
```

## Explain the Selection

```{index} Explain the Selection
```

A dynamic array supports fast indexed access and sequential reports. Linked storage makes known-node updates convenient but does not make locating a node free. Stacks and queues restrict access order. Balanced ordered collections support ordered lookup; a heap supports priority selection; a hash collection supports equality-based access.

For cancellation, the dictionary identifies active records while pending heap entries can become stale. Lazy deletion skips stale entries when removing them. This simple example forbids ID reuse during the batch; reuse or reprioritization needs a version policy. Treat that policy as an extension after ordinary dictionary and set operations, not as a prerequisite for understanding hashing.

```{index} A Set Answers Membership; a Count Answers Multiplicity
```

```{index} A Set Answers Membership; a Count Answers Multiplicity

## A Set Answers Membership; a Count Answers Multiplicity

Two departments submit product IDs for reconciliation. A set represents which IDs occur, regardless of how many times they were entered. A dictionary of counts represents how often each ID occurs. Choosing between them changes the information retained, not merely the syntax of the container.

Let the warehouse IDs be {A, B, C} and the sales IDs be {B, C, D}. Intersection gives IDs recognized by both: {B, C}. Warehouse minus sales gives {A}; sales minus warehouse gives {D}. The direction of difference matters. A union gives all recognized IDs {A, B, C, D}; it does not establish that either department's quantities agree.

| Question | Operation | Result for this example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which IDs are shared? | Intersection | B, C |
| Which warehouse IDs are absent from sales? | Warehouse minus sales | A |
| Which sales IDs are absent from warehouse? | Sales minus warehouse | D |
| Which IDs appear anywhere? | Union | A, B, C, D |

Now suppose sales submits B twice. A set still contains one B. That is correct for unique membership and wrong for a task that must detect repeated submissions. A frequency dictionary can increment B's count to two. State whether duplicates are errors, repeated events, or information to discard before building either representation.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

```{index} Choose Equality Before Comparing the Groups
```

```{index} Choose Equality Before Comparing the Groups
```

## Choose Equality Before Comparing the Groups

If product IDs are case-insensitive under the business contract, B and b must use compatible equality in both collections. Normalizing only one side can produce false missing-ID reports. For hashed keys, equal keys must have equal hash codes under the selected policy. A good hash distribution improves performance but cannot repair inconsistent equality.

Do not mutate fields that determine a key's hash/equality while that key is stored. The entry may remain physically present in a bucket chosen by its old meaning while a new lookup examines another location. Immutable key data or remove/change/reinsert workflows make that boundary explicit.

Set-operation APIs also have mutation contracts. Some operations modify the receiving set; query-based forms may produce a sequence instead. If the original warehouse membership must remain available, work on a copy or choose a nonmutating approach deliberately. Assigning another variable to the same set object does not create independent storage.

Guided exercise: add B twice and lowercase a once to the sales input. Produce two answers: a unique-ID reconciliation under a stated case policy and a repeated-ID report. Explain which information a set has discarded and why the frequency report cannot be reconstructed from that set alone.

Keyed access and membership answer different questions. A dictionary maps an ID to a record. A set records whether an ID belongs to a group. Business reconciliation often needs set operations as well as individual lookups.

Use the same equality rule for all collections that participate in one calculation. The examples use ordinal case-insensitive equality for submitted symbolic IDs and preserve original sets when a report needs several answers.

```{index} Sets and Frequency Counts
```

## Sets and Frequency Counts
```{index} HashSet; set; frequency count

A set stores keys without associated record values. Use `HashSet<T>.Add` to detect a first occurrence, or a dictionary to count occurrences. Give both the same comparer when they must agree about what counts as equal.

The set has two distinct statuses, and the counts are open three and closed two. The example prints keys in an explicit order; a hash collection's enumeration order is not a sorting contract. Sort keys separately when a report requires an order. Neither a set nor a dictionary supplies the priority-selection operation of a heap.

```{index} Union, Intersection, and Difference
```

## Union, Intersection, and Difference

```{index} Union, Intersection, and Difference
```

Let registered contain everyone registered for a workshop and attended contain everyone who checked in. Their intersection contains registered attendees. Registered minus attended identifies no-shows. Attended minus registered identifies walk-ins. Their union contains everyone appearing in either source.

HashSet operations such as IntersectWith and ExceptWith mutate the receiving set. Construct a copy first when you need to retain both source sets. Enumeration is not a sorted-report contract: copy to a list and sort explicitly for predictable output.

```{index} Lookup and Missing Values
```

## Lookup and Missing Values

```{index} Lookup and Missing Values
```

TryGetValue separates an absent key from a stored default value. Do not use a balance of zero, an empty owner name, or a null-like sentinel as an implicit membership test unless the contract explicitly excludes those values.

Choose Add when duplicate keys are errors; use indexer assignment when replacement is intended. If imports may repeat customer IDs, state whether a repeated row updates, accumulates, or rejects. Hashing provides access; it does not choose the business policy.

```{index} Keys Must Keep Their Meaning
```

## Keys Must Keep Their Meaning

```{index} Keys Must Keep Their Meaning
```

Do not change fields that determine a key's equality or hash while that key is stored. The key can become inconsistent with its original bucket. Immutable string IDs avoid that mutation hazard. A custom business object may instead need a comparer based on an immutable ID, as introduced in Chapter 13.

A hash collection does not provide sorted order, range queries, or next-priority removal. For those requirements choose another structure, or maintain multiple indexes with a clear consistency policy. The next section coordinates dictionary membership with the priority queue from Chapter 18.

```

```{index} A Collision Is Not Evidence That Keys Are Equal
```

```{index} A Collision Is Not Evidence That Keys Are Equal
```

## A Collision Is Not Evidence That Keys Are Equal

A hash function maps keys to a finite bucket range, so different keys can map to the same bucket. The hash narrows the search; equality identifies the actual key. In a table of five buckets using a simple remainder demonstration, integer keys 2, 7 and 12 all map to bucket two. Keeping only one value at that position would lose entries unless the ADT intentionally replaces an equal key.

A chained bucket can examine the entries for actual equality. An open-addressed representation follows a probe sequence instead. Removing an entry in open addressing must preserve the ability to find later entries whose probe passed through its slot. Turning a deleted slot directly into never-used can stop a search too soon; the distinction between deleted and never occupied matters.

Guided trace: insert the three colliding keys, remove seven, then find twelve. Explain why a search must still reach twelve. Now grow the bucket range and recompute placement; copying each entry to its old numeric slot is not sufficient because the mapping depends on the table size. Hash distribution, equality consistency, load and deletion policy work together.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

```{index} Dictionary Contracts and Key Equality
```

## Dictionary Contracts and Key Equality
```{index} dictionary; key equality; hashing

A dictionary associates one value with each distinct key. Looking up a customer ID asks for that ID's record; it does not ask for the first record in order. C# `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` uses hashing for key-based access. `Add` rejects an existing key, indexer assignment inserts or replaces, and `TryGetValue` reports whether a key exists without treating a missing key as a successful default value.

This dictionary treats `T-100` and `t-100` as equal, so assignment changes the owner rather than adding another key. Choose the equality policy when creating the collection and apply it consistently. For symbolic ticket IDs, ordinal comparison avoids culture-dependent language rules. This example deliberately ignores case; other applications may need case-sensitive identifiers.

Hashing and equality must agree: equal keys must have equal hash codes. Different keys may have the same hash code, so a lookup must still compare actual keys. A custom comparer supplies both operations. Do not modify fields that determine a stored key's equality or hash code; its new bucket may no longer match the location used during insertion. Strings are immutable, which avoids that particular mutation hazard. [Microsoft's GetHashCode contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode) explains this agreement.

```{index} Hash Codes and Bucket Mapping
```

## Hash Codes and Bucket Mapping
```{index} hash function; bucket; negative hash code

Separate two steps: compute an integer hash code, then map that code into one of m buckets. Hash codes can be negative. C# remainder can also be negative, and `Math.Abs(int.MinValue)` cannot fit in an `int`. Reinterpret the code as an unsigned integer before remainder to obtain a valid index without that overflow.

`unchecked((uint)hash)` keeps the original bits and interprets them as a nonnegative number; it does not claim that the code is a unique identifier. BucketCount must be positive. The result lies from zero through m - 1. Equal hash codes always map to the same bucket for a fixed m, but many different codes also map there.

String hash codes may vary across processes or platforms. Use them for temporary placement, not as permanent customer IDs or persisted checksums. The teaching map below uses integer IDs themselves as simple hash codes so its collision trace is reproducible. This is an illustration, not a general recommendation for distributing arbitrary business keys.

```{index} Separate Chaining and Complete Operations
```

## Separate Chaining and Complete Operations
```{index} separate chaining; collision; hash-table update

A collision occurs when different keys choose the same bucket. **Separate chaining** stores a collection of entries at each bucket. A lookup computes the bucket and compares keys within that chain. An update must search the chain before appending; otherwise it can create duplicate keys. Removal must preserve the other colliding entries.

With four buckets, IDs 101, 105, and 109 all choose bucket one. To find 109, inspect 101, then 105, then 109. To report that 113 is absent, inspect the entire chain. A successful lookup may stop early; an unsuccessful one must establish that no matching key exists.

The complete `TicketMap` stores integer ticket IDs and string owners. `Put` returns true for a new key and false for replacement. `Remove` reports whether membership changed. `TryGetValue` returns false on absence; ignore its output value in that case.

replacement inserted=False, count=3
after growth: buckets=8, count=4
0:  | 1: 105, 113 | 2:  | 3:  | 4:  | 5: 101, 109 | 6:  | 7:

source:
Each stored entry belongs to the bucket computed from its ID and the current bucket count. Count equals the total number of entries, and each ID occurs once. The internal entries are immutable; replacement installs a new entry with the same ID. An update returns before increasing Count or testing growth because it adds no key.

After removal, another colliding ID remains reachable in the same chain. Our chains are lists, so removal may shift later entries within that chain. The cost depends on chain length rather than the total number of buckets. This map keeps capacity after deletions and has no iterator API; production libraries provide more policies and interfaces.

```{index} Load Factor and Rehashing
```

## Load Factor and Rehashing
```{index} load factor; resizing; rehashing

Define load factor α = n / m, where n is the number of entries and m is the number of buckets. Before adding 113, the map has three entries in four buckets, so α = 0.75. A fourth new key would exceed the teaching threshold, so the map doubles to eight buckets before inserting it.

Changing the bucket count changes placement. Copying old bucket lists to the same array indexes is insufficient. Recompute every entry's bucket under the new capacity, a process called **rehashing**.

| ID | Bucket with m = 4 | Bucket with m = 8 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 101 | 1 | 5 |
| 105 | 1 | 1 |
| 109 | 1 | 5 |
| 113 | 1 | 1 |

Growth splits this collision group into two chains. It does not guarantee that all collisions disappear. A poor hash function can keep many keys in one chain even at low load factor.

Under well-distributed hashes and constant-time hashing/equality, chaining operations have expected O(1 + α) work. A pathological chain can require O(n) work. This resize visits all entries and initializes a larger bucket array, giving O(n + m) work for that operation. Geometric growth contributes amortized constant work per new key when load is kept bounded; one growth-triggering insertion can still be linear.

The threshold 0.75 belongs to this teaching map, not to a universal hash-table rule. Separate chaining permits α greater than one. Open addressing needs unused slots and becomes much more expensive as occupancy approaches one. Key hashing itself is an additional cost, such as scanning characters in a long string.

```{index} Open Addressing and Deleted Slots
```

## Open Addressing and Deleted Slots
```{index} open addressing; linear probing; tombstone

**Open addressing** stores entries directly in the table. **Linear probing** tries the chosen slot, then subsequent slots with wraparound until it finds the key or a place to insert. A lookup may stop at a slot that has never been occupied, because insertion would have stopped there too. It cannot stop merely because a previous entry was removed.

For capacity seven, IDs 10, 17, and 24 all start at slot three. Linear probing stores them at three, four, and five. Clearing slot three after deleting 10 would make a naive search for 17 stop early. A **tombstone** marks a deleted slot through which lookup must continue.

Limit a search to at most m probes so a full table cannot cause an endless loop. Insertion can reuse a tombstone, but it must still search far enough to rule out an existing equal key. Otherwise it can add a duplicate before reaching the old copy. Over time, many tombstones lengthen searches; rebuilding the table can remove them.

This example demonstrates a deletion rule, not a complete open-addressed dictionary. The chapter's complete implementation uses chaining. Both strategies must combine placement with actual key equality; neither treats a collision as a duplicate by itself.

The complete teaching map uses separate chaining. The probing/tombstone example is an optional comparison, not another full map implementation you must build. The next section applies dictionary and set contracts to business reconciliation.

# Hash Collections and Sets

Fast lookup depends on what it means for two keys to be the same. This chapter connects equality policies and hash codes to collisions, resizing, dictionaries, sets, and frequency counts. You will choose collections for reconciliation and coordinated-index workloads and explain how to preserve consistency when records change.

- **Key equality**: Decide which identifiers represent the same key.
- **Hashing**: Map keys to buckets and resolve collisions without confusing them with equality.
- **Growth**: Keep load and rehashing costs visible as the collection expands.
- **Sets and counts**: Distinguish membership from how many times a value appears.
- **Coordinated indexes**: Keep multiple collection views consistent under updates.

## Unneeded Constructor Code Exercise
```{index} Unneeded Constructor Code Exercise

Recall that objects are always initialized. Each instance variable
has a default value assigned before a constructor is even run.
The default value for numeric instance variables is 0, so the
call to `Clear` in the constructor could be left out, leaving the
body of the constructor empty! Try commenting that line out
and test that the behavior of demo program is the same.

Emphasizing the fact that you are thinking about the
initial values of instance variables is not a bad idea. Hence
a common practice is to
explicitly assign even the default values in the constructor, as
we did initially with the call to `Clear` inside the constructor.

If no constructor definition is explicitly provided at all,
the compiler implicitly creates one with no parameters and an empty body.
This means that the entire constructor in `Averager` could be omitted.
Comment the whole constructor out and check.

There is a defensive programming
reason to provide even the do-nothing constructor explicitly:
If you use the implicit constructor and then decide to add a constructor
with parameters, the implicit constructor is no longer defined by the compiler,
so any remaining call to it in your code becomes an error.

## Overview

To understand class and object-oriented programming (OOP), some important basic concepts learn first inlcude:

- **Class**: A class is a blueprint, prototype, or template.
- **Class Members**: In C#, a class contains members, which include **fields**, properties, **methods**, and events.
- **Class Instance**: An `object` is an `instance` of a class. Namely, an object is created based on a
  class and therefore is an instance of that class. An object can be created using the `new` keyword.

There are related terminology that you will see about class and OOP:

- **Field**: A field is a variable of any type that is declared directly in a class or struct. Fields are
  members of their containing type. A field stores a piece of data within an object. It acts like a
  variable and may have a different value for each instance of a type. [1]
- **Property**: Properties expose fields. Fields should (almost always) be kept private to a class and accessed via
  get and set properties.
- The **this** Keyword: In C#, the this keyword refers to the current instance of a class.
- **Reference Types**: A type that is defined as a class is a reference type. Other types include: interface, struct, delegate, or enum.
- **Constructor**: In C#, a constructor is called when an object is created to set default values. A constructor must have the
  **same name** as the enclosing class. Using constructor is not obligatory in C#. If no constructors are specified in a class, the compiler
  automatically creates a parameterless constructor.

```{index} Declaring Classes

## Declaring Classes

To declare a class, you need to use the `class` keyword and give a unique `identifier` (name) to the class. For example,
you want to create a customer class to include some data and methods in one unit:

```csharp
// [access modifier] - [class] - [identifier]

public class Customer
{
   // Fields, properties, methods and events go here...
}
```

Attributes to be considered when creating a class include:

- Access Modifiers: The default access for a class type is internal. Basic levels of access for a class include [2] :  
  - **public**: Access is not restricted. Anyone code can create instances of this class.
  - **protected**: Access is limited to the containing class or types derived from the containing class.
  - **internal**: Access is limited to the current assembly. [3]
  - **private**: Access is limited to the containing type.

- Class Identifier: A unique name for the class. An identifier is the name you assign to a type (class, interface, struct, delegate, or enum),
  member, variable, or namespace. An identifier begins with a letter or underscore. As a convention, use PascalCase for class names and method names.

- Class Body: The class body is surrounded by { }. The behavior and data are defined in the class body, including **fields**, properties, **methods**, and events on a class and
  are collectively referred to as **class members**.

- Base Class or Super Class: Optional. Name of the class’s superclass; preceded by a colon (:).

- Interfaces: Interface names implemented by the class; preceded by a colon (:).

## Beyond Getters and Setters

```{index} Averager; incremental average; running sum

Thus far we have had very simple classes with instance variables and
getter and setter methods, and maybe a ToString method.
These classes were designed to introduce the basic syntax for
classes with instances. The classes have just been containers for data
that we can read back, and change if there are setter methods - pretty
boring and limited. Many objects have more extensive behaviors, so we will
take a small step and imagine a somewhat more complicated `Averager` class:

- A new `Averager` starts with no data acknowledged.
- Be able to enter data values one at a time (method `AddDatum`).
  We will use `double` values.
- At any point be able to return the average of the numbers entered so far
  (method `GetAverage`).
  The average is the sum of all the values divided by number of values.
  With `double` values we assume a `double` average.
  This does not make sense if there
  are no values so far, but with double type we can use the value
  `NaN` (Not a Number) in this case.
- Be able to return the number of data elements entered so far
  (method `GetDataCount`)
- Be able to clear the `Averager`, going back to no data elements
  considered yet, like in a new `Averager` (method `Clear`)
- It is good to have a `ToString` method. We choose to have
  it label the number of data items and the average of the items.

The object starts from a fixed
state (no data) so we do not need any constructor parameters.

We can imagine a demonstration class `AveragerDemo` with a `Main` method
containing

```csharp
using System;
namespace IntroCS
{
   class AveragerDemo
   {
      public static void Main()
      {  // body chunk
         Averager a = new Averager();
         Console.WriteLine("New Averager: " + a);
         foreach (double x in new[] {5.1, -7.3, 11.0, 3.7}) {
            Console.WriteLine ("Next datum " + x);
            a.AddDatum (x);
            Console.WriteLine("average {0:G15} with {1} data values",
                              a.GetAverage(), a.GetDataCount());
         }
         a.Clear();
         Console.WriteLine("After clearing:");
         Console.WriteLine("average {0:G15} with {1} data values",
                           a.GetAverage(), a.GetDataCount());
      }                            // end chunk
   }
}


```

Next datum -7.3

Next datum 11
average 2.93333333333333 with 3 data values
Next datum 3.7
average 3.125 with 4 data values
After clearing:

```

Now that we have a clear idea of the proposed outward behavior, we
can consider how to implement the `Averager` class.

We could store a list of all the data values entered in any instance,
requiring a large amount of memory for a long list. However, this
functionality was built into early calculators, with very limited memory.
How can we do it without remembering the whole list?
Consider a concrete example:

If I have entered numbers 2.1, 4.5 and 5.4, and want the average, it is

> {math}`(2.1+4.5+5.4)/3=12.0/3=4.0`

If I want to include a further number 5.0, the average becomes

> {math}`(2.1+4.5+5.4+5.0)/4=17.0/4=4.25`

Note the relationship to the previous average expression:

> {math}`=((2.1+4.5+5.4)+5.0)/4=(12.0+5.0)/(3+1)`

In the numerator we have added the latest value to the previous sum,
and in the denominator the count of data items is increased by one.
All we need to remember to
go on to include the next item is the sum of values so far and the
number of values so far. We can just have instance variables
`sum` and `dataCount`.

## Keep the Boundary of the Best K Items

A sales report needs the largest three amounts from a stream. Sorting every amount is one possible solution, but the requested result is smaller than the full sorted input. A min-heap of the currently retained best three exposes the weakest retained amount at its root. That is exactly the boundary a new candidate must beat.

For amounts 7, 2, 9, 4, 10, retain 7, 2 and 9 first. Their minimum is 2. Candidate 4 replaces 2; candidate 10 replaces the new minimum 4. The retained values are 7, 9 and 10. Their heap storage need not be printed in sorted report order; sorting only the final retained values is a separate reporting step.

| Candidate | Decision | Retained values as a set of amounts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7, 2, 9 | Fill three places | 2, 7, 9 |
| 4 | Replace the smallest retained amount | 4, 7, 9 |
| 10 | Replace the smallest retained amount | 7, 9, 10 |

After each processed prefix, the heap contains the best min(k, processed count) entries under the chosen comparison policy. If a new candidate is no better than the root and the heap is full, at least k retained entries are already as good, so discarding it preserves the invariant. If it is better, replacing the weakest retained entry restores the best-k claim. This argument explains the algorithm rather than just observing a successful result.

Decide whether k zero is a valid request, what to do when fewer than k entries exist, and how tied amounts affect which record IDs are retained. Keeping amounts alone loses record identity. A report requiring deterministic tie order needs a secondary policy, not an assumption about library heap stability.

Priority also differs from fairness. A permanently urgent stream can delay ordinary requests indefinitely even when each minimum-priority removal is correct. Aging, reserved service opportunities or another explicit scheduling policy may be needed. That is a requirement choice layered on the structure, not a defect fixed by reversing the heap comparison.

Guided variation: select the smallest three amounts instead. Explain why a max-heap exposes the weakest retained boundary for that goal. Then retain complete invoice records with equal amounts and state what additional information your comparison must use if arrival order breaks ties.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

A priority queue is useful when the next item is chosen by urgency or score rather than arrival position. Use a clearly stated tie rule for service work and a clearly stated retained-set rule for top-k reporting.

The following applications use the library queue so you can focus on the workload. The heap implementation in the previous section explains the repair work behind this behavior. A dictionary-based cancellation index is introduced only after hash collections in the next chapter.

```{index} Top-K with a Min-Heap
```

## Top-K with a Min-Heap
```{index} top-k; min-heap; streaming

Keep the k largest observed transaction amounts without sorting the entire input. Maintain at most k retained values in a min-heap. The root is the smallest retained value, so it is the candidate to discard when a larger value arrives.

**Invariant:** after each input, the heap contains the largest `min(k, valuesSeen)` values of that prefix, including repeated values. If fewer than k values are stored, add the next value. Once full, a value no larger than the root cannot improve the retained multiset; a larger one replaces that root.

For k = 3, retained values after the first three inputs are 72, 84, 91. Processing 99 drops 72; 67 changes nothing; 88 drops 84; 95 drops 88; the second 95 drops 91. The final result is `99, 95, 95`. Repeated equal amounts remain separate observations.

For n inputs and positive k, maintenance has an O(n log(k + 1)) upper bound and O(k) storage, or fewer entries when n < k. Producing the final ordered result costs O(k log(k + 1)) in the worst case. k = 0 returns immediately; negative k is rejected. If record identity or tie order matters, include an explicit secondary priority and define which tied records to retain.

# Priority Queues and Heaps

The next service request may be the most urgent rather than the earliest arrival. This chapter separates a priority queue's removal contract from a heap's representation, then develops insertion and removal repairs. You will test heap invariants and apply bounded priority selection to top-k workloads while distinguishing priority from fairness.

- **Priority queue**: Choose the next item by priority rather than arrival order.
- **Binary heap**: Combine complete-tree shape with a parent-child order invariant.
- **Sift repair**: Restore order along one affected path after an update.
- **Tie policy**: State what happens when primary priorities are equal.
- **Top-k selection**: Keep a bounded set of the most relevant items.

## Priority Describes Removal, Not a Fully Sorted Array

A service desk chooses the lowest numbered priority next. That is a removal contract. It does not require that every stored element be maintained in complete sorted order, nor does it say that equal priorities must leave in arrival order. State the priority direction and tie policy before interpreting a printed storage array.

A min-heap requires each parent's priority to be no greater than its children's. The root is therefore a minimum, but siblings need not be ordered. In the array [1, 4, 2, 7, 6, 3], the values 4 and 2 can appear in that order without violating the heap. Reading the array from left to right is not the same as repeatedly removing the minimum.

| Operation needed | Heap property helps with it? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inspect the minimum | Yes | It is at the root |
| Remove the minimum and restore the property | Yes | Only a repair path is needed |
| Print everything in sorted order without changing storage | Not directly | Heap order is weaker than total order |
| Find an arbitrary ID | Not directly | Priority ancestry does not locate arbitrary keys |

The complete-tree shape lets an array encode parent/child positions without one node object per edge. With zero-based positions, a non-root index i has parent (i-1)/2 using integer division; its potential children are 2i+1 and 2i+2. A child position must still be checked against Count. Capacity is not the number of live heap entries.

Then compare positions one and two: their values are out of sorted-array order but are allowed as siblings. ## Priority Queue Behavior

```{index} priority queue
```

A **priority queue** removes the item with the next priority, not necessarily the item that arrived first. In C#'s `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>`, lower priority values come out first by default.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Respond to outage
Reset password
Process invoice
Send summary

source: The outage has priority `0`, so it is processed before lower-urgency work. Priority queues are useful for schedulers, event simulations, pathfinding, triage, and any workflow where "next" means most important rather than oldest.

A priority queue defines how you select the next element. It does not promise that enumeration is sorted or that arbitrary keys are easy to locate. The numerical priority has an application meaning: here zero is most urgent. Dequeue from an empty queue is an error; `TryDequeue` reports false instead.

Equal priorities need a policy. The .NET library does not guarantee arrival order for ties. If the service desk requires first-arrived service among equally urgent tickets, use the pair `(urgency, arrivalNumber)` as the priority. Tuple comparison considers urgency first and arrival second. Each arrival number is unique within the queue, so the resulting order is deterministic.

The order is T-101, T-100, T-102. A later urgent ticket can move ahead, while equal-urgency tickets retain their arrival order. The queue alone does not prevent starvation if urgent work arrives indefinitely. Fairness requires an additional scheduling policy.

The manual implementation in this section is a **binary** heap. The current .NET `PriorityQueue` uses four children per parent internally. Its API behavior is the same priority-queue idea, but the binary index formulas below describe the teaching implementation, not the library's internal layout. [Microsoft's PriorityQueue documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.priorityqueue-2) describes both tie behavior and the library representation.

## Heap Representation

```{index} heap; min-heap; complete tree
```

A **heap** is a common priority-queue representation. A binary heap has two key rules:

- **Shape rule**: the tree is complete, filled level by level from left to right.
- **Order rule**: in a min-heap, each parent priority is less than or equal to its child priorities.

Because the shape is complete, a heap can be stored compactly in an array. For an item at index `i`, the children are at `2 * i + 1` and `2 * i + 2`.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
1 -> left child 3
1 -> right child 2
3 -> left child 7
3 -> right child 5
2 -> left child 6
2 -> right child 4

source: The array is not fully sorted. It only guarantees that each parent is no larger than its children. That weaker rule is enough to keep the minimum at the root.

For a non-root index i, its parent is `(i - 1) / 2`, using integer division. Valid child indexes must be less than Count. Count describes occupied positions; the backing array may have extra capacity that is not part of the heap.

```text
          1 (0)
        /       \
     3 (1)     2 (2)
    /    \     /    \
 7 (3) 5 (4) 6 (5) 4 (6)
```

The values obey parent-child order, but siblings and separate subtrees can be out of numerical order. For example, 3 precedes 2 in the array. Repeatedly removing the root produces a sorted sequence; reading the raw array does not. The complete shape guarantees height Θ(log n) for a nonempty binary heap.

A priority queue is an access rule. The next section implements it with a binary heap, while application code may use the library PriorityQueue. Enumeration is not a sorted report; repeated removal is the operation whose priority order is specified.

## Repair Only the Part an Operation Can Disturb

Enqueue adds a new entry at the next open leaf position so the complete shape is preserved. All old parent-child relations are unchanged. Only the new entry's path toward the root can violate min-heap order. Bubble-up compares with the parent and swaps while the child is smaller. Moving upward strictly decreases its index, so repair terminates.

Start with [2, 5, 4] and enqueue 1. Appending produces [2, 5, 4, 1]. Comparing 1 with parent 5 gives [2, 1, 4, 5]. Comparing that 1 with root 2 gives [1, 2, 4, 5]. Do not sort the whole array; that would enforce a stronger and more expensive condition than the operation needs.

Dequeue first saves the root result. Move the last live entry to the root and reduce Count. The only possible ordering defects now lie downward from that replacement. Choose the smaller existing child before swapping; exchanging with an arbitrary child can leave a smaller sibling above a larger parent relation.

| Heap after removing 1 | Inspection | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [5, 2, 4] | Children 2 and 4 | Choose 2 |
| [2, 5, 4] | 5 has no child | Stop |

A singleton removal needs no child access after Count becomes zero. An empty removal must follow the stated failure policy without first reading position zero. Also clear unused reference slots when the implementation owns a backing array and should release references to removed objects. Reducing Count hides a slot from the abstract sequence, but it does not itself erase a stored reference.

The height of a complete heap is logarithmic in its live size, which bounds the number of repair levels. Array growth can add copying to an enqueue, so qualify an operation's cost rather than ignoring representation maintenance. Bulk building by bottom-up repair is a related algorithm with a different aggregate argument; it is not proved merely by multiplying one operation's bound.

Guided exercise: repeat enqueue with a value 6 that already belongs below its parent. Predict how many swaps occur and distinguish swaps from comparisons. Then remove down to empty and enqueue again. Those cases test both the invariant and whether endpoint handling leaves the structure reusable.

## Enqueue and Bubble Up

```{index} heap; bubble up
```
To insert into a heap, place the new item at the end to preserve the complete-tree shape, then **bubble up** while it violates the heap order rule.
The new value `0` starts at the end. It swaps with larger parents until the min-heap property is restored.

Trace the appended zero from index seven to the root:

| Stage | Index path | Array |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Append | 7 | 1, 3, 2, 7, 5, 6, 4, 0 |
| Swap with 7 | 7 → 3 | 1, 3, 2, 0, 5, 6, 4, 7 |
| Swap with 3 | 3 → 1 | 1, 0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 4, 7 |
| Swap with 1 | 1 → 0 | 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 4, 7 |

Before insertion, every old parent-child relation satisfies the order rule. Appending adds only one possible violation between the new item and its parent. Each swap repairs that relation and moves the possible violation upward. Stop at the root or when the parent is no larger. This explains why repairing one path is sufficient.

```{index} Dequeue and Sink Down
```

## Dequeue and Sink Down

```{index} heap; sink down
```
To remove the minimum item, remove the root, move the last item to the root, then **sink down** until the heap order rule is restored.
Both bubble-up and sink-down follow one root-to-leaf path, so their work grows with heap height, not with every item in the heap.

In the removal example, replacing root 1 with the last value 4 gives `4, 3, 2, 7, 5, 6`. Compare both children before choosing the swap: 2 is smaller than 3, so swap indexes zero and two. The result is `2, 3, 4, 7, 5, 6`. The next child is 6; 4 is already no larger, so stop.

Choosing a larger child can leave the root larger than the other child. Sink-down must choose the smaller existing child and handle a last parent with only a left child. Removing the last array position preserves the complete shape. For a singleton, removal leaves no root to repair.

The complete generic heap below hides the backing list and accepts an optional comparer. The element type must support the default ordering, or you must supply a comparer. `Peek` and `Dequeue` throw on empty; `TryDequeue` distinguishes empty from a stored default value. Equal values are legal, but this heap does not impose stable arrival order on equal comparisons.

`List<T>` grows its storage when necessary. Bubble-up uses O(log n) comparisons, but a single enqueue that copies a full backing array can take O(n) time. Across a long sequence, storage growth contributes amortized O(1) per append; enqueue therefore has amortized O(log(n + 1)) time. Dequeue repairs at most one downward path and takes O(log(n + 1)); it does not shrink this backing list. Peek and Count take O(1). The iterative repair uses O(1) extra space, while the stored items use O(n) space.

`IsValid` scans all parent-child relations, so it takes Θ(n) time. It is a diagnostic method, not part of every production operation. `Snapshot` also takes Θ(n) time and space to copy the occupied values. Checking the minimum alone would miss a violation inside a subtree. Test empty and singleton states, duplicate priorities, an odd final child, ascending/descending input, draining, and reuse.

A heap can also be built from an existing array by sinking internal nodes from right to left. Most nodes are near leaves and require little repair; summing that work gives O(n) bottom-up construction. Repeated insertion has an O(n log n) worst-case bound. This chapter implements repeated enqueue first; bottom-up construction is an extension.

# Dynamic Programming and Backtracking Repeated subproblems invite reuse; a tree of choices requires careful exploration and undo. This chapter connects memoization and tabulation to complete state definitions, optimization recurrences, reconstructed solutions, and backtracking. You will compare reusable-pack planning with one-use record selection and report resource-limited searches honestly. - **Overlapping subproblems**: The same smaller problem appears repeatedly. - **Optimal substructure**: A larger solution can be built from smaller optimal solutions. - **Memoization**: A top-down technique that stores recursive results for reuse. - **Tabulation**: A bottom-up technique that fills a table from small cases to large cases. - **Backtracking**: A search pattern that makes a choice, explores it, then undoes the choice.

## Undo Exactly the Choice Owned by the Current Call

Backtracking explores alternatives while preserving enough state to return to a previous decision point. For one-use invoice reconciliation, each position can be included or excluded. A helper at position i with remaining target r represents a particular smaller problem: can some subset of positions i onward total r? Both i and r matter because they describe which choices remain.

For amounts 2, 3 and 5 with target five, one witness is 2 plus 3 and another is 5 alone. Choosing the first invoice changes the remaining target from five to three and advances the position. Excluding it leaves target five but still advances the position. If both branches kept the same position, the program could reuse an invoice whose contract permits only one use.

| Branch from position 0 | Next position | Remaining target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Include amount 2 | 1 | 3 |
| Exclude amount 2 | 1 | 5 |

When building a selected-position list, add the position for the include branch, explore, and remove that same choice when returning to explore an alternative. A saved result must be a snapshot if later mutations would otherwise change it. Assigning a result variable to the mutable working list only creates another reference to the changing list.

Signed amounts require care with pruning. The common shortcut remaining target below zero means impossible is unsafe when later negative adjustments can reduce a sum. Bounds based on the sums of remaining negative and positive amounts provide a justified possible range. Prune only when the requested remaining value lies outside that range. Pruning changes how much is explored; it must not discard a feasible solution.

Caching failed states can avoid revisiting the same impossible suffix/target pair. The cache key must identify the complete state under the fixed input and policy. A call budget is a separate implementation limit: exhausting it means the search did not finish, not that infeasibility has been proved. Preserve this distinction when reporting results to a user.

Guided trace: add a -2 adjustment after a temporarily excessive positive choice. Construct a target for which pruning on a negative remainder would lose a valid witness. Then compare a proven failed state with a stopped-by-budget state. Explain why only the former may safely be reused as evidence of impossibility.

## Backtracking and Search Spaces

Backtracking is depth-first search through decisions. An invariant describes the partial choice; a base case records a complete result; undo restores shared state before a sibling branch. Pruning must exclude only impossible branches. Returning a witness allows the caller to check the decision.

```{index} Choose, Explore, Undo, and Snapshot
```

## Choose, Explore, Undo, and Snapshot
```{index} Choose, Explore, Undo, and Snapshot

At position i, chosen holds exactly the included positions from 0..i−1. Include i, recurse to i+1, undo, then exclude i. At i=n, snapshot chosen. Positions distinguish equal-valued business records; choosing position zero twice is not allowed.

The include/exclude branches are disjoint and exhaustive, and each step reduces unprocessed positions, proving termination and completeness. Copying at a leaf prevents later undo from erasing saved results. There are 2^n leaves and 2^(n+1)−1 recursive calls. Total copied position entries are n·2^(n−1) for n≥1: enumeration takes Θ(n2^n) time and retained output space, even though the active stack and chosen list use only O(n). The teaching API limits n to 16 to bound retained output. Empty input has one subset, the empty subset.

```{index} One-Use Subset Sum Needs a Two-Part State
```

## One-Use Subset Sum Needs a Two-Part State
```{index} One-Use Subset Sum Needs a Two-Part State

For signed invoice adjustments, ask whether some distinct positions sum to target. State (i,r) means: using only positions i..n−1, can we make remaining r? Include gives (i+1,r−value[i]); exclude gives (i+1,r). A zero remainder accepts the current subset, including the empty subset for target zero.

Each call advances i, so no position is reused and recursion terminates. The shared chosen list contains selected earlier positions; remaining equals target minus their sum. The implementation snapshots a successful witness and restores the list even on early success or a search-budget exception. A null witness means proven infeasibility; an empty witness is a feasible zero target. Use long sums and remaining amounts so two int values do not overflow.

```{index} Prove Bounds Before Pruning
```

## Prove Bounds Before Pruning
```{index} Prove Bounds Before Pruning

The rule remaining<0 is safe for nonnegative values because future additions cannot decrease the chosen sum. It fails for signed values: 8 followed by −3 makes five after temporarily overshooting. For a signed suffix define L(i) as the sum of its negative values and U(i) as the sum of its positive values. Every suffix subset sum lies in [L(i),U(i)]. Prune only if r lies outside those bounds. Being inside the interval does not guarantee feasibility.

Compute suffix bounds once in O(n) time/storage. The code checks success before suffix exhaustion, preserves both branches when necessary, and accepts zeros. The initial total bound check also runs in the unpruned comparison to avoid subtracting from an extreme impossible long target. Branch order affects measured calls when the search stops at its first witness; pruning has no universal speedup guarantee.

```{index} Memoize Failed States Without Losing Choices
```

## Memoize Failed States Without Losing Choices
```{index} Memoize Failed States Without Losing Choices

Two different prefixes can leave the same (i,r). Their future feasibility is identical because the remaining positions and target are identical. Cache a state only after both branches fail. Do not cache only r: the same remaining amount with different inventories is a different question. Keeping only failed states avoids needing to store a prefix-dependent witness.

For nonnegative values and target T, reachable non-pruned remainder states lie in 0..T, so there are O(n(T+1)) possible states. Signed inputs instead depend on the attainable sum range, which can be large. Expected constant-time hash lookup gives work proportional to visited states/transitions plus pruning and terminal calls. Without effective caching or pruning, worst-case branching is O(2^n), with O(n) active stack/path space. This teaching implementation accepts up to 128 positions and a default million-call budget. Exhausting it throws with feasibility unknown; it must never return false as though the instance were solved.

```{index} Permutations Use Every Position Exactly Once
```

## Permutations Use Every Position Exactly Once
```{index} Permutations Use Every Position Exactly Once

At each depth choose an unused position. Maintain used[i] exactly when i appears in order, and undo both structures. Labels can repeat while positions remain distinct. This is useful when two jobs share a display name but have different IDs.

There are n! position permutations; copying each length-n order requires Θ(n·n!) time and retained output space. Active state is O(n). The API caps n at eight for materialized results. Generating unique value permutations is a different contract and would need deliberate duplicate suppression. A streamed generator can reduce retained storage, but cannot eliminate the cost of producing all requested outputs.

## Derive Every Entry of a Small Purchasing Plan

A purchaser can use unlimited packs containing one, three or four items and needs exactly six items. Largest-first gives 4+1+1, but 3+3 uses fewer packs. Dynamic programming improves the choice by comparing every legal final pack, not by repeatedly taking the largest.

Let best[a] be the minimum number of packs totaling a. Best[0]=0 represents the valid empty purchase. For each positive a, consider a final pack c with c≤a. Only reachable best[a-c] entries can supply candidates; their count plus one is a possible answer. Store both the lowest count and the chosen last pack. Null means unreachable, not zero packs.

| Amount a | Reachable candidates using last pack 1, 3, 4 | best[a] | Chosen last pack |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | Base case | 0 | None |
| 1 | best[0]+1=1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | best[1]+1=2 | 2 | 1 |
| 3 | best[2]+1=3; best[0]+1=1 | 1 | 3 |
| 4 | best[3]+1=2; best[1]+1=2; best[0]+1=1 | 1 | 4 |
| 5 | best[4]+1=2; best[2]+1=3; best[1]+1=2 | 2 | 1 |
| 6 | best[5]+1=3; best[3]+1=2; best[2]+1=3 | 2 | 3 |

The tie at amount five preserves last pack one when denominations are visited in ascending order and updates require a strict improvement. This is a deterministic witness policy; it does not change the optimum count. The following focused code uses a fixed valid input to expose the table updates. The retained full API performs validation and resource-bound checks.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Amount 1: count 1, last 1
Amount 2: count 2, last 1
Amount 3: count 1, last 3
Amount 4: count 1, last 4
Amount 5: count 2, last 1
Amount 6: count 2, last 3
Plan: 3+3

source:
Read the recurrence in the code: amount-pack selects the smaller state; previous+1 accounts for the final pack; the comparison retains the best candidate. A positive pack makes the dependency strictly smaller, so increasing amounts are a valid evaluation order. Zero or negative denominations would invalidate this reasoning and are rejected by the full API.

Reconstruction follows decisions backwards, not all table entries in descending order. For six, last[6]=3, so append three and continue with remaining three. Last[3]=3 reaches remaining zero. The two chosen packs sum to six and their count equals best[6]. A valid plan proves feasibility; the recurrence's comparison of all final choices establishes optimality.

Remove denomination one and ask for five using only three and four. Fill best[0] through best[5] before running a program. Do not initialize all counts to zero: that would make impossible remainders appear reachable.

```{dropdown} Check the smaller table
The counts are 0, null, null, 1, 1, null. Five is unreachable because neither remainder two nor remainder one is reachable. No reconstruction should start from five. Target zero is different: its count is zero and its valid plan is empty.
```

Now compare two records each worth three with unlimited denomination three. A target of nine is reachable with unlimited packs, but not from two one-use records. ## Define the State from the Choices That Remain

A purchasing team can buy unlimited packs of sizes one, three and four and wants exactly six units using the fewest packs. Greedily taking four first leaves two one-unit packs, for three packs total. Two packs of three use only two packs. The counterexample shows that a locally largest pack is not a generally safe choice for this objective.

Let B(a) be the minimum number of packs for amount a. The base is B(0)=0. To solve a positive amount, consider every permitted last pack c and a reachable predecessor amount a-c. A candidate solution has one more pack than B(a-c). Choose the minimum candidate. This considers the last step of every feasible optimum, rather than guessing which first pack looks largest.

| Amount | Best count for sizes 1,3,4 | One predecessor choice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | Empty solution |
| 1 | 1 | 0 plus 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 plus 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 plus 3 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 plus 4 |
| 5 | 2 | 1 plus 4, or another optimal tie |
| 6 | 2 | 3 plus 3 |

Optimal substructure supplies the justification: removing the last pack from an optimal solution leaves an optimal solution to the predecessor amount. If a better predecessor existed, appending the same last pack would improve the supposed optimum. Positive pack sizes make predecessor amounts smaller, giving a valid tabulation order and terminating reconstruction.

## Preserve Enough Information to Explain the Answer

An optimum count is not the same output as an actual purchasing plan. Store a predecessor choice when an amount is improved, then walk backward to zero to reconstruct a witness. Validate that the witness sums to the requested amount and has the reported number of packs. If no predecessor is feasible, represent unreachable distinctly from the valid zero-pack solution at amount zero.

The state depends on inventory assumptions. If each invoice or pack position can be used only once, amount alone does not identify the remaining options. Chapter 25's backtracking lesson uses both a position and remaining target. Reusing an amount-only unlimited-pack recurrence for limited inventory can return an impossible plan.

Guided variation: remove size one and request five from sizes three and four. Explain why zero is not a valid optimum count for this request and why reconstruction must not loop forever through an invented predecessor. Then request zero and distinguish that valid empty solution from the unreachable positive amount. The preserved verification cases check both objective value and witness.

## Minimum Coins: Model Before Implementation
```{index} Minimum Coins: Model Before Implementation

A purchasing system uses unlimited packs of sizes 1,3,4. Minimize the number of packs totaling target six. Let B(a) be the minimum count for a; B(0)=0, and B(a)=min(1+B(a−c)) over positive denominations c≤a whose remainder is reachable. If no such predecessor exists, a is unreachable. Removing the last coin from any optimal plan leaves an optimal remainder plan: a better remainder would improve the original plan.

Positive denominations ensure a−c<a, so amounts in increasing order satisfy dependencies and reconstruction strictly decreases remaining amount. Nullable count distinguishes unreachable from a valid zero-coin plan. Duplicate denominations are normalized; ascending denominations and strict improvement make equal-count ties deterministic. Empty denominations can make only zero. Reject zero/negative coins: a zero coin breaks progress and a negative coin changes the state graph. The table invariant is that all smaller amounts have correct optima or correct unreachable markers; considering every possible last coin establishes the next entry.

```{index} State Size, Numeric Size, and the Requested Result
```

## State Size, Numeric Size, and the Requested Result
```{index} State Size, Numeric Size, and the Requested Result

With target T and D input denominations, sorting/normalization costs O(D log(D+1)); filling the table costs O(Td) for d distinct denominations, and table storage is O(T). Reconstructing K chosen coins adds O(K) output space and time. This implementation caps T at one million as an explicit allocation policy. These costs depend on the numeric target, not just the number of digits encoding it: the method is pseudo-polynomial.

Memoization can avoid some states reachable from the requested state; tabulation can avoid recursion and simplify dependency order. Neither is universally better. An amount-only coin state is sufficient for unlimited coins. If each pack is available once, remaining inventory matters: amount alone loses essential information. Chapter 25’s subset search uses (position, remaining), which preserves which items are still available. Rolling storage also trades away reconstruction information unless another recovery method is supplied.

## Compare Three Executions of the Same Dependency Rule

A repeated subproblem is a question with the same complete state, not just a similarly named function call. With F(0)=0, F(1)=1 and F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2), the integer n fully identifies the question. Fix that definition before sharing results. Changing the base values creates a different sequence and invalidates an old cache.

For F(4), the naive call tree asks for F(3) and F(2). F(3) asks for F(2) and F(1), so F(2) is expanded twice. Termination is already guaranteed by decreasing n; the problem is repeated work.

```text
F(4)
  F(3)
    F(2)
      F(1)
      F(0)
    F(1)
  F(2)
    F(1)
    F(0)
```

There are nine invocations including base cases. Only four calls are simultaneously active on the deepest path. A cache can remove repeated expansion without turning the recursion into constant-depth execution.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Store F(2)=1
Store F(3)=2
Hit F(2)=1
Store F(4)=3
F(4)=3; calls=7; hits=1; computed=3

source:
The cell intentionally calls only a fixed valid argument. The complete APIs below retain domain and resource limits. Base cases are returned directly rather than stored; therefore computed counts non-base cache misses, not every call. Cache F(2) only after both dependencies return, otherwise another call could read an incomplete result.

| Event during F(4) | Completed cache afterward | Significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finish F(2) within F(3) | 2→1 | First non-base state completed |
| Finish F(3) | 2→1, 3→2 | Its dependencies were available |
| Request F(2) from F(4) | Unchanged | Cache hit avoids another expansion |
| Finish F(4) | 2→1, 3→2, 4→3 | Requested result is now complete |

For n≥2, there are n-1 distinct non-base states. Each is expanded once and makes two recursive calls, so total invocations are the initial call plus twice the number of expansions: 2n-1. For n=4 this is seven. Exact counts depend on this implementation's decision not to cache base cases; the linear growth claim does not depend on adopting this exact convention.

## Fill the Same States Without Recursive Calls

Tabulation stores the same mathematical answers but selects an order explicitly. For increasing i, both i-1 and i-2 already exist. Initialization supplies F(0) and F(1); it is not an incidental convenience. The small cell below makes every completed table entry visible.

## Save Answers to Repeated Questions, Not Arbitrary Intermediate State

Fibonacci gives a small example where termination alone does not prevent repeated work. Computing F(5) asks for F(4) and F(3); computing F(4) asks for F(3) again. A cache can retain the completed answer for a numeric argument and reuse it when that same subproblem returns. The key is sufficient because the recurrence and base cases are fixed for this computation.

Memoization starts from the requested state and recursively solves missing dependencies. Tabulation chooses an order in which needed dependencies have already been solved. For Fibonacci, increasing argument order works because F(i) depends on smaller arguments. These are two execution strategies for a stated dependency structure, not two unrelated tricks for making code faster.

| i | F(i) | Dependencies already available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | Base case |
| 1 | 1 | Base case |
| 2 | 1 | F(1), F(0) |
| 3 | 2 | F(2), F(1) |
| 4 | 3 | F(3), F(2) |
| 5 | 5 | F(4), F(3) |

The table invariant is that every earlier stored entry has its correct specified value before the next entry is computed. Storing a result before all dependencies have been completed can cache a partial value as if it were final. Reusing one global cache across requests with different policies can likewise mix different problems under the same key.

Rolling storage keeps only the two predecessor values when only the final Fibonacci result is required. It cannot simultaneously promise to return all earlier table entries without retaining or recomputing them. This is a tradeoff between requested output and retained state. Memoization also does not eliminate recursive stack depth simply because repeated arithmetic has been removed.

```

## Memoization and Tabulation

A state identifies one smaller problem. A transition relates it to other states. Define the state, base cases, legal inputs, dependency order, and returned result before choosing a cache or table. Counting problems such as Fibonacci need a decomposition; minimum-coin optimization additionally needs optimal substructure.

```{index} Repeated Work Is Visible
```

## Repeated Work Is Visible
```{index} Repeated Work Is Visible

F(0)=0, F(1)=1, and F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for n≥2. The argument strictly decreases, but the recursion tree repeats arguments. Count every invocation, including base cases; computed counts only non-base expansions. Compare the same n, not unrelated examples.

The naive call recurrence is C(0)=C(1)=1 and C(n)=1+C(n−1)+C(n−2); C(n)=2F(n+1)−1. Calls are exponential in n while active stack depth is Θ(n). This teaching implementation caps naive n at 25 to keep browser runs short; all Fibonacci APIs otherwise accept 0..92, the range that fits signed long. Invalid n is rejected before recursion.

```{index} Memoization Stores Complete States
```

## Memoization Stores Complete States
```{index} Memoization Stores Complete States

The cache key n fully identifies F(n) because the recurrence and base cases are fixed. Every cached value is a completed correct result. Compute a missing state recursively, then store it. Local cache ownership avoids mixing unrelated requests or caller-supplied incorrect entries.

For n≥2 there are n−1 distinct non-base states, 2n−1 calls including cache hits, and max(0,n−3) hits. Base results are not cached here. Expected constant-time dictionary lookup gives Θ(n) time, Θ(n) cache storage, and Θ(n) stack space. These are distinct costs. A fresh invocation starts a fresh cache; memoization does not make the recursive stack disappear. Induction proves correctness: bases are correct, recursive dependencies are smaller, and their sum is F(n).

```{index} Tabulation Follows Dependency Order
```

## Tabulation Follows Dependency Order
```{index} Tabulation Follows Dependency Order

The invariant before iteration i is that entries 0..i−1 equal their specified Fibonacci values. Writing table[i] from i−1 and i−2 preserves it. Initialize entry one only when it exists; zero must work.

A full table costs Θ(n) time and Θ(n) storage without recursion. Rolling state keeps only the two needed predecessors, giving Θ(n) time and Θ(1) auxiliary storage when only the final value is requested. It cannot provide every historical table entry. Checked addition protects arithmetic; validating 0..92 also avoids computing an unnecessary F(93) on the final rolling update.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```

# Privacy and Security in Code
Optional practice extends Chapter 1.2 after methods, decisions, iteration, and text processing. Use it when handling personal data in files or logs. The database appendix develops parameterized SQL.

Business programs handle **personal data**: names, email addresses, phone numbers, card numbers, birth dates, and purchase histories. Personal data is any information that identifies a person or can be linked to one. Mishandling it harms the people it describes and exposes the organization to legal penalties. This section turns privacy and security principles into small coding habits you can use now.

```{index} privacy; law
```

```{index} Personal Data and the Law
```

## Personal Data and the Law

Privacy laws differ by place, but they share common ideas. Three examples:

- **GDPR** (EU Regulation 2016/679, applies from May 25, 2018) sets principles for processing personal data, including *purpose limitation* (use data only for the stated purpose), *data minimisation* (collect only what is needed), and *storage limitation* (do not keep it longer than needed).[^0905_privacy_security-gdpr]
- **CCPA** (California Consumer Privacy Act, in effect since January 1, 2020, and expanded by the CPRA from January 1, 2023) gives California residents rights to know about, delete, and opt out of the sale of their personal information.[^0905_privacy_security-ccpa]
- **FERPA** (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974) protects the privacy of student education records in the United States, including your grades in this course.[^0905_privacy_security-ferpa]

You do not need to be a lawyer to follow the habits these laws have in common: **collect less, show less, and keep less.**

```{index} masking; personal data
```

```{index} Show Less: Masking
```

## Show Less: Masking

Many screens and documents need only enough of a value to recognize it. A support agent confirming an account needs to see `a***@example.com`, not the full address. Masking uses the string methods from {ref}`string-methods`:
Receipts and order confirmations conventionally show only the last four digits of a card:
Masking is for display. A program that does not need a value at all should not collect or store it in the first place.

```{index} untrusted input; validation
```

```{index} Treat Every Input as Untrusted
```

## Treat Every Input as Untrusted

Every value that comes from outside the program, such as keyboard input, a file, a web form, or another system, may be wrong by accident or on purpose. Check both the **type** and the **business rule** before using it. `int.TryParse` from Chapter 6 handles the type; an `if` handles the range:

A missing check can do more than produce a wrong answer: the OWASP Top 10, a widely used list of the most serious web application security risks, includes Broken Access Control (A01) and Injection (A05) in its 2025 edition.[^0905_privacy_security-owasp]

```{index} Logging Without Leaking
```

## Logging Without Leaking

Logs record what a program did so people can investigate problems later. Logs are also read by many people and kept for a long time, so they must not contain secrets such as passwords or full card numbers:

Three related principles guide secure design:

- **Confidentiality, integrity, availability.** Keep data from people who should not see it, keep it from being changed improperly, and keep the system usable for those who need it.
- **Least privilege.** Give each user and program only the access its task requires. A report that only reads orders should not be able to delete them.
- **Never store passwords.** Systems store a salted, slow *hash* of a password: a one-way value that can check a password without revealing it. Use a well-tested library for this; never write your own.

```{index} privacy; summary
```

```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

Personal data deserves care in every line of code that touches it. Collect, show, and keep only what a task needs; mask values for display; check every input for type and business rules; never build commands from input text; and keep secrets out of logs. These habits match the principles that privacy laws such as GDPR, CCPA, and FERPA share.

## Treat Each Imported Line as a Small Contract

An inventory file contains code, quantity and unit price separated by commas. Splitting a line gives pieces of text; it does not prove that there are exactly three fields, that a quantity is an integer, or that a price is nonnegative. Work from the schema toward conversion, not from a convenient Parse call toward assumptions about everything that came before it.

For a deliberately simple format without quoted separators, process a line through distinct stages. Preserve the original text and line number so that a rejected record can be explained. First count fields, then normalize only fields whose rules permit it, then parse numeric representations, and finally check the business domain. A zero quantity may be allowed even when an empty quantity field is not.

| Line | First relevant result |
| --- | --- |
| PEN,3,1.25 | Three fields; numeric and domain checks can proceed |
| PEN,three,1.25 | Quantity representation is invalid |
| PEN,-3,1.25 | Quantity is numeric but violates a nonnegative rule |
| PEN,3 | Schema is incomplete |

The order matters. Indexing the third field before checking field count can throw instead of producing a useful rejection. Normalizing every character in the entire line can alter meaningful free text. Catching every exception can hide a programming defect such as an incorrect index as though it were bad source data.

A regular expression can describe the shape of one field, such as a fixed prefix followed by digits. It does not replace business validation. A code may match a shape and still refer to an unknown product. For a small fixed delimiter format, Split and ordinary conditions may be easier to understand. The supporting regex reading develops groups, replacement and pattern-specific syntax; use a pattern only after stating what language of text it should accept.

## Read a Pattern as a Description of Accepted Text

A product label consists of two uppercase ASCII letters, a hyphen and four digits. Before choosing regular-expression symbols, write accepted and rejected examples. AB-0042 fits; A-0042 has too few letters; AB-42 has too few digits; and a larger sentence containing AB-0042 is not itself one complete label. This last distinction separates finding a matching substring from validating an entire field.

For this deliberately narrow label, the pattern `\A[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}\z` uses beginning/end-of-input anchors, a range of letters repeated twice, a literal hyphen and four ASCII digits. It states shape, not whether AB is a known department. In a C# verbatim string literal the pattern can be written `@"\A[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}\z"`; ordinary C# string escaping and regex escaping are different layers. The @ belongs to the string literal form, not to the regex language.

| Pattern part | Meaning under this contract |
| --- | --- |
| \A | Beginning of the input |
| [A-Z]{2} | Exactly two letters from the stated ASCII range |
| - | The separator |
| [0-9]{4} | Exactly four ASCII digits |
| \z | End of the input |

A group such as `(?<number>[0-9]{4})` names a captured part. Extracting number as text retains leading zeros; converting it to an integer would answer a different question. Check whether a match succeeded before treating group contents as a valid field. A match object exists even when the match is unsuccessful, so object existence alone is not the success test.

Regex replacement also has a policy. Removing every nondigit character may produce a digit-only result while silently discarding an unexpected department or separator. Decide whether malformed input should be repaired, rejected or retained with a warning. A cleaning rule is not equivalent to a validation rule.

Guided exercise: test AB-0042, AB-0042 followed by a newline, lowercase ab-0042, a matching code embedded in a sentence and an empty string. Predict results under the exact anchored policy above. Then change the requirement to finding labels inside messages and explain which anchors must change. Do not broaden the policy merely because one difficult input fails. For untrusted complex patterns and long inputs, consider bounded matching behavior; the core fixed-shape examples do not teach arbitrary patterns as safe substitutes for a parser.
