```{index} Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost
```

## Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost

For nine appends, the trace copies `2 + 4 + 8 = 14` existing entries and writes nine new entries. Counting these array writes gives 23 writes across nine operations. Some individual appends are costly, but the total grows in proportion to the number of appends.

For a longer sequence, copy sizes form `2 + 4 + 8 + ...`. Each term is twice the previous one, so the sum stays below twice the final number of inserted items. Adding one write per appended item still gives a total proportional to `n`. Dividing total work by `n` gives a constant amortized cost. This is a bound over an operation sequence, not an assumption about random inputs.

Growing by one slot each time would copy `2 + 3 + 4 + ... + (n - 1)` entries. That total grows quadratically. Avoiding spare capacity would therefore make repeated appends progressively expensive.

The tradeoff is spare storage. Doubling leaves unused slots after growth, and a resize temporarily keeps both old and new arrays alive. Amortized O(1) also does not guarantee a short pause for every append. A system with a strict response deadline may reserve capacity ahead of time.

# Arrays and Linked Lists A resizable product list and a chain of linked nodes can represent the same sequence while doing very different work. This chapter develops both representations and compares access, growth, insertion, and removal under explicit invariants. You will test the sequence contract and justify a representation for a workload; Chapter 16 develops search and sorting algorithms separately. - **Contiguous storage**: Array-backed sequences keep elements next to each other for fast indexed access. - **Dynamic array**: A dynamic array grows by allocating larger storage and copying existing values. - **Linked node**: A linked structure stores values in nodes connected by references. - **Insertion and deletion**: Different representations make middle updates cheaper or more expensive. - **Performance tradeoff**: Choosing a sequence representation depends on access, growth, and update patterns.

# Linked Nodes

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

A linked list stores a sequence as separate node objects connected by references. The representation makes insertion and deletion local, but finding a position requires traversal.

```{index} node
```
```{index} linked list
```

```{index} Nodes and References
```

## Nodes and References

Each node stores a value and a reference to the next node.

```text
head -> [10 | next] -> [20 | next] -> [30 | null]
```

The list variable stores a reference to the first node, often called the **head**. The last node points to `null`.

```{index} traversal; linked list
```

```{index} Traversal
```

## Traversal
A linked list cannot jump directly to index `7`. To find an item, code follows references one node at a time. This is called **traversal**.

```{index} insertion; linked list
```

```{index} Insertion After a Node
```

## Insertion After a Node

If you already have a reference to a node, inserting after it is local. Create a new node, point it to the old next node, then point the current node to the new node.

```text
before: [A] -> [C]
after:  [A] -> [B] -> [C]
```

```{index} deletion; linked list
```

```{index} Deletion After a Node
```

## Deletion After a Node

Deleting after a known node is also local. Skip over the next node by changing one reference.

```text
before: [A] -> [B] -> [C]
after:  [A] --------> [C]
```

```{index} Costs and Tradeoffs
```

```{index} Costs and Tradeoffs
```

## Costs and Tradeoffs

Linked lists make some updates cheap only after the position is known.

| Operation | Singly linked list cost |
| --- | --- |
| Read first item | O(1) |
| Traverse all items | O(n) |
| Find by value | O(n) |
| Insert after known node | O(1) |
| Delete after known node | O(1) |
| Read by index | O(n) |

The phrase "known node" matters. If the program must search for the node first, that search is part of the total cost.

```{index} alias; linked list; reference
```

```{index} References Are Paths, Not Copies
```

## References Are Paths, Not Copies

Work orders may also be represented by separate node objects. A node's `Next` is a reference to another node, not an embedded copy of the remaining list. Assigning `current = head` copies a reference: both variables initially identify the same object. Changing `current` to `current.Next` moves a cursor without moving `head`.

```text
head ----> [WO-10 | next] ---> [WO-30 | null]
current --^
```

If you traverse by repeatedly assigning to `head`, you lose your entry point to the sequence. A separate cursor preserves the list. Also distinguish changing a reference from changing an object: setting `current = current.Next` moves the cursor; setting `current.Next = ...` changes a link in the sequence.

**Trace (basic):** Draw both arrows before and after one cursor advance. Which variable still reaches the first work order?

```{index} linked list; insertion invariant; cycle
```

```{index} Insertion Order and Lost Links
```

## Insertion Order and Lost Links

You know the node for `WO-10` and want to insert `WO-20` before `WO-30`. Preserve the old successor before overwriting its only incoming list link.

| Step | References | What remains reachable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create B | `A.Next = C`, `B.Next = null` | A still reaches C. |
| Save successor | `B.Next = A.Next` | B now reaches C too. |
| Connect B | `A.Next = B` | A reaches B, then C. |

The correct two assignments are `inserted.Next = node.Next; node.Next = inserted;`. Reversing them makes `inserted.Next` refer to `inserted` itself. The result is a cycle, and the original successor is disconnected from this chain. A traversal waiting for `null` would never finish.

For an empty list there is no predecessor. Inserting at the front sets `newNode.Next = head` before replacing `head`. The same steps work when the old head is null. A list wrapper is useful because it owns the head reference and can update it safely.

**Debug (applied):** Explain the reversed-assignment bug using named nodes A, B, and C. Do not run an unbounded traversal of the broken chain.

```{index} Removal, Head, and Tail Invariants
```

## Removal, Head, and Tail Invariants

To remove B after A, preserve B's successor by setting `A.Next = B.Next`. Removing the first node instead requires `head = head.Next`, because there is no preceding node to update. Unlinking does not destroy the object immediately: other references might still reach it, and .NET manages reclamation of unreachable objects.

A wrapper with a tail reference must maintain these rules:

- An empty list has count zero and both head and tail null.
- A nonempty list has a reachable head and tail, and `tail.Next` is null.
- Following `Next` from head visits exactly `Count` nodes and reaches tail last.

Removing the only node must clear both endpoints. Removing the last node of a longer chain must move tail to the predecessor. A tail reference makes append constant-time but does not make removal of the last node constant-time: a singly linked list still has to find that predecessor.

## A Complete Singly Linked Sequence

This wrapper presents the same `Add`, `Insert`, indexer, and `RemoveAt` operations as the dynamic array. Nodes are private so client code cannot accidentally create cycles or change count without updating the wrapper.

`NodeAt` validates the index, then follows links. `head!` and `Next!` express facts established by the list invariants after validation; they do not create runtime null checks. If those invariants are broken, the suppression cannot repair them.

Run the cell independently. It inserts the middle order, removes the head, empties the list, and appends again. The last line should be `count=1, first=WO-40`.

Notice that the interface hides implementation choices. `Insert(1, value)` first locates the predecessor and then rewires links. Although the rewiring is O(1), this index-based operation is O(n) in the worst case. The earlier `InsertAfter` example had a different assumption: its caller already held a node reference.

The demonstration prints by repeated indexing only because the list is tiny. For a long linked list, that pattern repeats traversal: indexes zero through `n - 1` require roughly `0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1)` link advances. A cursor or iterator should visit the sequence once instead.

## Doubly Linked Lists: A Different Tradeoff

A doubly linked node stores both `Next` and `Previous`. A known node can therefore find its predecessor without a search, and a stored tail can support constant-time removal at the end. The price is another reference per node and more links to maintain.

```text
null <- [A] <-> [B] <-> [C] -> null
```

Removing B connects `A.Next` to C and `C.Previous` to A. Removing an endpoint also changes the wrapper's head or tail. This representation still does not provide direct indexing: to find a numeric position, follow links from an endpoint.

We have explored several ways of storing a collection of the same type of data:

- arrays: built-in syntax, unchanging size of the collection
- List: generic class type, allows the size of the collection to grow

Both approaches allow reference to data elements using a
numerical index between square brackets, as in `words[i]`.
The index provides an order for the elements,
but there is no meaning to the index beyond the sequence order.

Sometimes, we want to look up data based on a more meaningful key, as in a
dictionary: given a word, you can look up the definition.

C# uses the type name [Dictionary](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2?view=net-8.0), but with greater generality than in
nontechnical use. In a regular dictionary, you start with a word,
and look up the definition. The generalization is to have some piece of
data that leads you to (or *maps* to) another piece of data.
The computer science jargon is that a **key** leads you to a **value**.
In a normal dictionary, these are both likely to be strings, but in the
C# generalization, the possible types of key and value are much more extensive.
Hence the generic `Dictionary` type requires you to specify
*both a type for the key and a type for the value*.

A stock clerk knows a product code, not its position in a list. Searching for that code and coordinating a separate quantity list is unnecessary work when the program can directly associate the code with its quantity. The big idea is a **key-to-value association**. Retrieval, updating stock, and counting repeated requests all reuse that association.

Keep three questions separate: Is the key present? What value belongs to it? Does this operation insert a new entry or update an existing one? Keys identify entries; they are not sequence positions. The examples below retain the translation dictionary, then transfer the same pattern to counting.

Arrays are fine if you know ahead of time how long your sequence of items is.
Then you create your array with that length, and you are all set.

If you want a variable sized container, you are likely to want a `List`.
List is a type of collection that is used when the number of elements is unknown.

The big idea is a **resizable ordered sequence**: `List<T>` provides indexed positions while managing changes in size.

Follow one distinction throughout this lesson: changing a value at an existing position is an update; inserting or removing an item changes the sequence and can change later positions. Use the operation comparison in {ref}`collection-operation-syntax` as a map while learning these calls.

## Lists Basics

A `List<T>` starts with an element type and then supports the everyday sequence operations you expect: add an item, count the items, read an item by index, and loop through the items. The index rules are the same as arrays: the first item is at index `0`.

A list can also be initialized with values. A `for` loop is useful when the index is part of the output or logic; a `foreach` loop is simpler when you only need each value.

`Count` is the number of stored elements. `Capacity` is the number of positions reserved internally before another growth allocation is needed; it can exceed `Count`. `Clear()` removes the elements but normally keeps that reserved capacity. Use `Count` for valid element indexes, not `Capacity`. You do not need to tune capacity for the examples in this chapter.

## Common Pitfall: Modifying a List While Iterating

`foreach` keeps an internal position in the list as it loops. Adding or removing elements through that same list while a `foreach` is still running invalidates that position, and C# detects it: the loop throws an `InvalidOperationException` rather than silently skipping or duplicating elements.

outputs.name: stdout

## Read an Operation as a State Change and a Result

The family map tells you which question a collection can answer. Now describe an operation with three parts: what must already be true, what changes, and what result the caller receives. This makes the cross-family tables below more useful than a list of names to memorize.

Consider the sequence of product codes PEN, PAD, PEN. Removing by value selects an occurrence matching a value; removing by index selects a position. Popping a stack or dequeuing a queue selects according to processing order instead. Even when each operation reduces a count by one, it need not select the same element. Compare the selection rule before comparing the method spelling.

| Intended action | Information supplied | Question to ask before calling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove a known product code from a list | Value | Which matching occurrence is removed? |
| Remove the third list position | Index 2 | Does that position exist now? |
| Take the next queued request | No identifying key | Is the queue nonempty? |
| Find stock for a product code | Key | What happens when that key is absent? |

Returning a value and mutating a collection are independent possibilities. A lookup can return a result without removing anything. A removal can both change storage and report success. A Try-style operation supplies a Boolean success signal so that an absent result can be distinguished from a legitimate default value. Read both the success flag and the output value under the documented contract.

Traversal is also an operation with a contract. Foreach provides a shared language form, but it does not make the collection families share one universal order. A sequence has positional order; a work queue has a service policy; a keyed collection has its own enumeration guarantees. If a report requires sorted product codes, request or construct that order explicitly instead of assuming that lookup storage supplies it.

Replacing a value is not changing the length of the same array.

## Generic Collections

```{index} generic type; type parameter; type argument; type safety
```

A collection's **family** tells you how it organizes access. Its **element type** tells you what values it stores. These are separate choices: a list of integers and a list of strings use the same sequence operations, but they store different kinds of values.

A **generic type** is defined using one or more **type parameters**, which are placeholders for types. In documentation, `List<T>` means a list whose element type is represented by `T`. When you write `List<string>`, `string` is the **type argument** you have supplied for that parameter. The library provides the reusable class; you choose its type arguments when declaring the collection.

| Library notation | Example in a program | Meaning of the type arguments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `List<T>` | `List<string>` | Each element is a string. |
| `HashSet<T>` | `HashSet<int>` | Each distinct element is an integer. |
| `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` | `Dictionary<string, int>` | Keys are strings; values are integers. |
| `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>` | `PriorityQueue<string, int>` | Elements are strings; priorities are integers. |

Generic collections provide **type safety**: the compiler checks whether supplied values can be used as the declared types. A `List<int>` accepts integers; it will not accept the string `"twelve"`. This catches a mismatch before the program runs. It does not establish that every integer is appropriate: a negative stock quantity is still an integer, so business validation remains your responsibility.

```{index} The Standard Library and Namespaces
```

### The Standard Library and Namespaces

```{index} namespace; standard library; System.Collections.Generic
```

A **namespace** groups related type names. Most collection classes demonstrated here belong to `System.Collections.Generic`. The `using System.Collections.Generic;` directive lets you write `List<string>` instead of the full name `System.Collections.Generic.List<string>`. It makes names available; it does not create a collection or download a package.

Creating a collection requires constructing an object, as in `new List<string>()`. The parentheses call a **constructor**, which initializes the new object. You will study constructors and your own class definitions in Chapter 10. For now, you are using classes already supplied by the library, just as earlier examples used library methods.

Some modern C# projects import common namespaces automatically. Every runnable example here includes the imports it needs so you can run it independently. The following diagram shows three collection namespaces you may encounter, rather than a complete inventory of .NET collections.

:::{figure} ../../figures/collection_namespaces.svg
:width: 700

Selected .NET collection namespaces: generic collections, older non-generic collections, and concurrent collections.
:::

Prefer the generic collection classes for new code like the examples in this chapter. Older non-generic types, such as `ArrayList` and `Hashtable`, commonly store values through `object` and do not provide the same element-type checking. Recognizing their names can help you read older programs; learning them is not a separate requirement here.

Other library collections address additional needs. Sorted dictionaries and sorted sets maintain ordering by key or element, rather than merely remembering positions. Concurrent collections support coordinated access from multiple threads. Immutable collections produce updated versions without changing the original collection. These are additional dimensions of collection design, not extra families that you must master in this lesson.

## Similar Operations, Different Methods

```{index} collection; operation comparison; method call; property; indexer

```{index} Put In, Inspect, and Take Out

### Put In, Inspect, and Take Out

```{index} Add; Remove; RemoveAt; Push; Pop; Peek; Enqueue; Dequeue
```

The following table shows calls on variables named for their collection family. `item`, `key`, `value`, `index`, and `priority` represent values already available to the program. These calls are alternatives for different types, not one interchangeable API.

| Family | Put an item in | Inspect or retrieve | Take an item out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array, `T[]` | Fill an existing position: `array[index] = item` | `array[index]` | No operation shrinks this same array. |
| List, `List<T>` | `list.Add(item)`; `list.Insert(index, item)` | `list[index]` | `list.Remove(item)`; `list.RemoveAt(index)` |
| Linked list, `LinkedList<T>` | `linked.AddFirst(item)`; `linked.AddLast(item)` | `linked.First.Value` or `linked.Last.Value`, when nonempty | `linked.Remove(item)`; `linked.RemoveFirst()`; `linked.RemoveLast()` |
| Dictionary, `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` | `dictionary.Add(key, value)` | `dictionary[key]`, when the key exists | `dictionary.Remove(key)` |
| Set, `HashSet<T>` | `set.Add(item)` | `set.Contains(item)` tests membership | `set.Remove(item)` |
| Stack, `Stack<T>` | `stack.Push(item)` | `stack.Peek()` inspects the top | `stack.Pop()` removes **and returns** the top |
| Queue, `Queue<T>` | `queue.Enqueue(item)` | `queue.Peek()` inspects the front | `queue.Dequeue()` removes **and returns** the front |
| Priority queue, `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>` | `priorityQueue.Enqueue(item, priority)` | `priorityQueue.Peek()` inspects the next item | `priorityQueue.Dequeue()` removes **and returns** the next item |

`Add`, `Push`, and `Enqueue` all put an item into a collection, but they express different access policies. `Remove`, `Pop`, and `Dequeue` all remove something, but they do not select it in the same way or return the same kind of result. `Peek` reads the next item without removing it. With the default priority comparer, a lower priority value is selected first; equal priorities do not guarantee arrival order.

For a list, `Remove(item)` removes the first equal item and returns a Boolean indicating success. `RemoveAt(index)` removes the item at a position and returns no value. For an integer list, this distinction matters: `Remove(2)` searches for the **value** 2, whereas `RemoveAt(2)` selects the **third position**. A set's `Add` returns `false` for a duplicate. A dictionary's `Add` rejects a duplicate key, while `dictionary[key] = value` inserts a missing key or replaces its current value. Similar names do not guarantee identical behavior.

An array's fixed length is part of its contract. Replacing a slot is an update, not insertion; setting it to zero or null does not remove the slot. Creating another array or using a resizable list is a different operation.

```{index} Size, Membership, and Safe Access
```

### Size, Membership, and Safe Access

```{index} Count; Length; Contains; ContainsKey; TryGetValue; TryPop; TryDequeue
```

| Family | How many items? | Is this item or key present? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Array | `array.Length` | `Array.IndexOf(array, item) >= 0` for a one-dimensional array |
| List | `list.Count` | `list.Contains(item)` |
| Linked list | `linked.Count` | `linked.Contains(item)` |
| Dictionary | `dictionary.Count` | `dictionary.ContainsKey(key)` |
| Set | `set.Count` | `set.Contains(item)` |
| Stack | `stack.Count` | `stack.Contains(item)` |
| Queue | `queue.Count` | `queue.Contains(item)` |
| Priority queue | `priorityQueue.Count` | No direct `Contains` method; searching entries is a separate task. |

A membership test answers whether an item exists, not how quickly the search runs. The family demonstrations explain the different access patterns. `foreach` visits elements across these families, but its traversal order follows each type's contract; enumerating a priority queue is not guaranteed to produce priority order.

Before indexing an array or list, check the valid range. Before reading `linked.First.Value`, check that a first node exists. Before calling `Peek`, `Pop`, or `Dequeue`, consider the empty case. These calls throw when no item is available. The library also offers Boolean-returning alternatives: `TryPeek`, `TryPop` for stacks, and `TryDequeue` for queues. Priority queues offer `TryPeek` and `TryDequeue` with both element and priority outputs. Dictionaries offer `TryGetValue` for a key that might be absent.

Their general pattern is:

```text
if (dictionary.TryGetValue(key, out valueType value))
{
    // Use value only after the lookup succeeds.
}
```

`out` allows the method to supply a value through an argument. Here the Boolean result tells the `if` whether the lookup succeeded. Section 8.4 develops this lookup pattern with runnable examples. You do not need to memorize every `Try` signature now; recognize the shared idea of checking success before using a result.

**Make the connections:** A basket needs to add and remove a chosen item; an undo history needs to remove the most recent action; a service line needs to remove the earliest arrival. Explain why these related needs lead to `Add`/`Remove`, `Push`/`Pop`, and `Enqueue`/`Dequeue`. Then identify which operations change size and which only inspect data. ### Arrays and Lists

```{index} array; list; index; sequence
```

A **sequence** gives its elements positions. In the arrays and lists used here, positions are indexed from zero. Both can contain repeated values. Their order is the order of the sequence, which is not necessarily sorted order.

An array's length remains fixed after creation, but its elements can change. Fixed length does not mean read-only data. A list manages storage as elements are added or removed. Its `Count` reports the number of elements currently in the list; an array uses `Length`.

Read this example as a comparison of behavior. The weekly array still has five positions after a correction. The basket grows when a second item is added, and it retains the order of those additions.

source:
Use an array when a fixed number of indexed positions expresses the task clearly. Use a list when the sequence changes size during normal work. A list is not automatically the best choice simply because it is more flexible: the fixed five-day structure can make the meaning of the array clear. Likewise, repeatedly replacing arrays just to add another basket item makes ordinary work harder than it needs to be.

```

### Linked Lists

```{index} linked list; node
```

A **linked list** organizes a sequence as **nodes**, each holding an element and links to neighboring nodes. .NET's `LinkedList<T>` is doubly linked: a node can refer to both its previous and its next node. You do not use `steps[1]` to retrieve its second element. You traverse the sequence or work with a node reference.[^0801_collections-linked-list]

Imagine a sequence of order-processing steps. After locating the packing step, you discover that a gift-check step belongs immediately after it. In the example below, `AddLast` returns a reference to the new node; `AddAfter` uses that reference to choose an insertion point. `var` asks C# to infer the node variable's type from the returned value.

text:
Pack order
Check gift message
Dispatch order

source: The result is still an ordered sequence, but it has different access operations from an indexed list. Inserting beside a node you already hold avoids shifting later elements. Finding that node can still require a search, and nodes have storage overhead. A linked list is therefore not a universal replacement for `List<T>`. Chapter 14 develops these tradeoffs and their implementations.

```{index} Dictionaries
```

### Dictionaries

```{index} dictionary; key; value; key-value pair
```

A **dictionary** associates a **key**, which identifies an entry, with a **value**, which is the information stored for that key. A stock lookup might use a product code as the key and an integer quantity as the value. Unlike a list index, the code expresses identity rather than position.

Keys are unique within a dictionary: one key cannot identify two separate entries. Values do not have to be unique. Two products may have the same stock quantity without being the same product. Here both codes initially map to `12`, and the program retrieves a quantity by code.

The expression `stock["NOTEBOOK"]` asks for a value associated with a key. It does not ask for the first, second, or alphabetically earliest entry. A dictionary is not an alphabetically sorted list, and you should not make a report depend on its enumeration order. You also need a policy for unknown codes; Section 8.4 teaches safe lookup and the difference between adding an entry and updating one.

```{index} Sets
```

### Sets

```{index} set; membership; uniqueness
```

A **set** stores distinct elements and emphasizes **membership**, meaning whether an element is present. Adding an equal element again does not create another copy. A set therefore answers a different question from a list: "Which customers participated?" rather than "What were all the participation events?"

If a customer uses a promotion twice, a list can record both events, while a set can record that customer's participation once. In this demonstration, `Add` returns `false` for the repeated value because no new element was added. `Contains` asks whether an element is in the set.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Distinct customers: 2
Added C101 again: False
C205 participated: True

source:
A set does not preserve the number of times a value appeared. If you need that number, a dictionary can associate each customer with a count. A `HashSet<T>` also does not promise sorted enumeration. Chapter 19 explains hashing, equality, and set operations; here you only need to recognize the membership and uniqueness contract.

**Check Your Understanding:** A list contains the product codes `PEN`, `PEN`, and `NOTEBOOK`. Would a set be a suitable replacement for the basket? Would it be suitable for the distinct products included in a promotion report?

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
A set would lose the repeated PEN entry, so it would not preserve a basket that uses repeated entries to represent quantity. It would be suitable for a report asking only which distinct product codes appeared. The choice depends on whether duplicates carry information.
```

### Processing Order

```{index} processing order; stack; queue; priority queue
```

Sometimes the important question is which item should leave the collection next. A list lets you choose a position, but that freedom puts the responsibility for enforcing the processing rule on your program. A stack or queue expresses a particular rule through its operations.

These structures do not decide an organization's policy for you. If requests should be handled in arrival order, choose a collection that expresses that policy. If urgency should take precedence, make the urgency rule explicit and choose a different structure.

```{index} Stacks and Queues
```

### Stacks and Queues

```{index} last in first out; first in first out; push; pop; enqueue; dequeue
```

A **stack** follows **last in, first out (LIFO)**. `Push` adds an item at the top; `Pop` removes and returns the top item. Think of an undo history: the most recent action should normally be the first action undone. Storing a description of an action is only a demonstration of ordering; a real undo feature also needs a way to reverse that action.

A **queue** follows **first in, first out (FIFO)**. `Enqueue` adds an item at the back; `Dequeue` removes and returns the item at the front. This expresses an arrival-order service line.

Both collections below receive `Order A` followed by `Order B`. Predict which order each returns before running the example.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Stack returns: Order B
Queue returns: Order A
Actions remaining: 1
Orders remaining: 1

source:
Removing an item changes the collection: each now has one item left. `Peek` lets you inspect the next item without removing it. Removing from an empty stack or queue requires a separate check or a suitable `Try...` operation; this example establishes that both are nonempty before removal. Chapter 15 develops safe operations and practical applications.

The FIFO rule is an ordering rule, not a complete definition of fairness. For example, an arrival-order queue does not by itself accommodate an urgent safety issue. You still need to decide whether arrival order expresses the policy the task actually requires.

```{index} Priority Queues
```

### Priority Queues

```{index} priority queue; priority
```

A **priority queue** chooses the next item using a priority value rather than its arrival position. In .NET's default `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>`, the item with the **lowest priority value** is removed first. A smaller number therefore means earlier processing in this example. This is a convention you must define for the application, not an automatic interpretation of what "high priority" means.[^0801_collections-priority-queue]

Each insertion supplies two pieces of information: the element to store and its priority. A routine request arrives first, but the urgent request leaves first because its priority value is smaller.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Urgent replacement
Scheduled pickup
Routine restock

source:
The removed items follow the priority rule even though they arrived in another order. A priority queue does not guarantee FIFO order among items with equal priority. If arrival order must break ties, the application needs an explicit tie-breaking rule. The unique priorities in this example avoid that ambiguity. Chapter 18 develops priorities and heap implementations.

**Check Your Understanding:** Which collection fits each task: undo the latest edit, serve the earliest waiting request, or process the smallest urgency number first?

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
Use a stack for the latest edit, a queue for arrival-order requests, and a priority queue for the smallest urgency value. All three may store the same element type; the difference is the retrieval rule.
```

## Traversal and Shared References

```{index} traversal; enumeration; IEnumerable; reference; alias; mutation
```

**Traversal**, also called **enumeration**, means visiting a collection's elements. `foreach` provides familiar syntax for this work, but the order and the kind of element you receive depend on the collection. Arrays and lists follow their sequence order. A dictionary enumerates key/value entries. A set supports enumeration, but its purpose is membership rather than sorted traversal. `PriorityQueue` is a special case: it exposes an `UnorderedItems` view for enumeration instead of supporting `foreach` directly on the queue. That view does not promise priority order; use successive removals when you need that order.

The enumerable collection types demonstrated here implement `IEnumerable<T>`, an interface describing how to enumerate values.[^0801_collections-collection-interface] You do not need to write an interface to use these library collections. Later chapters explain how a type can provide this capability itself. Also distinguish traversal from removal: looping through a queue with `foreach` does not serve and remove its waiting items.

Here a traversal computes a total without changing the stored quantities. The accumulator starts at zero, so an empty list would produce a total of zero.

The mutable library collection classes shown here are **reference types**. A variable refers to a collection object. Assigning that variable to another variable copies the reference, rather than making a second collection. Two names for the same object are **aliases**. Arrays have reference behavior too; this continues the idea introduced in Chapter 7.

Consider a basket shown in two parts of a program. If both variables refer to the same basket, adding an item through one variable is visible through the other. If you need a separate snapshot of a list's elements, you must explicitly create a new collection.

`basket` and `sameBasket` refer to one list containing two strings. `snapshot` is a different list containing the one string that was present when it was created. This is a copy of the elements, not a general promise to duplicate every object an element might refer to. Chapter 11 revisits that distinction with objects and composition.

Mutation means changing an existing object's state, such as adding to a list. Reassigning a variable to a different list is a different action. This distinction matters when collections are passed to methods or shared between parts of a program. An operation can affect more code than the variable name immediately in front of you suggests.

You should also check whether an operation is valid during traversal. In particular, adding or removing list elements inside a `foreach` over that same list invalidates its enumeration. Section 8.3 shows a safe removal pattern. A short loop can still be incorrect if it ignores the collection's operating rules.

A small order contains quantities `2`, `1`, and `3`. The starter stores them in a `List<int>`. Compute the total with `foreach` and store that total under the key `"ORD-101"` in a `Dictionary<string, int>`. Print the entry count and the saved total. Expected output is `Line items: 3` and `Saved total: 6` on separate lines.

After running your code, explain why the quantities form a list and why the saved summary uses a dictionary. Change the list to be empty and predict both results before running it again.

The list stores a sequence of quantities, including any repeated quantities. The dictionary associates an order's identity with its total. With an empty list, the entry count and calculated total are both zero. The dictionary still has one entry because the program saves that zero total under `ORD-101`; no line items is different from no saved summary.

## Summary

Collections combine stored values with rules for using them. Arrays and lists provide indexed sequences; linked lists organize nodes; dictionaries support key-based lookup; sets emphasize uniqueness and membership; stacks, queues, and priority queues determine what comes next. Generic type arguments specify the types of stored elements, keys, values, or priorities.

Choose the collection by explaining the task's access pattern, ordering, duplicates, and changes in size. Then check the details of its contract. The following sections put that reasoning into practice with lists and dictionaries.

```{index} Data Collections ```

A bookstore handles many groups of values: the quantities sold during a week, the items in a customer's basket, stock quantities indexed by product code, and orders waiting for collection. Each group contains several values, but the program does different work with each one. Finding Tuesday's sales, looking up a product code, and selecting the next order are different questions. The way you organize the values should support the question you need to answer.

A **collection** groups values and provides operations for working with them. Arrays are the first collection type we studied: {doc}`Chapter 7 <../07_arrays/0700_arrays>` introduced fixed-length, indexed sequences. Keeping that chapter separate gave us time to practice indexing, traversal, and multidimensional data. It did not put arrays outside the collection category. This chapter broadens our choices to other ready-made collection types in the .NET standard library. These classes are often called **built-in collections** because they come with .NET, although they are library types used by C#, rather than separate C# language features. Arrays have direct C# language syntax, such as `int[]`; collection classes such as `List<int>` are library types. Both belong in our collection-family comparison.

This section introduces the big ideas before the detailed syntax: what a collection promises, how values can be accessed, and how to choose among collection families. You will see eight useful families and small demonstrations of their behavior. The next two sections develop `List<T>` and `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` in depth. For the other families, your goal here is to recognize the need they address and predict their basic behavior, not to memorize every method or implement a data structure.

**Reading path:** First explain the access question, compare the families, and connect their operations. Work through arrays/lists, dictionaries, and shared references before the order-summary exercise. Use the linked-list, set, stack/queue, and priority-queue demonstrations to recognize their policies; their implementations and detailed APIs belong to later chapters. The operation tables are references to revisit, not a list of signatures to memorize in one sitting.

## Collections and Operations

```{index} collection; element; collection operation; data structure
```

An **element** is one item stored in a collection. An array of sales quantities has numbers as its elements; a list of product codes has strings. A dictionary stores entries that associate a key with a value. The surrounding collection gives these items an organization and a set of supported actions.

Several operations recur across collection families:

| Operation | Question it answers | Bookstore example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add or insert | How does a new item enter the group? | Add a product code to the current basket. |
| Retrieve | How do you obtain a particular item? | Find the stock quantity associated with a product code. |
| Update | How does stored information change? | Replace a recorded quantity after a stock check. |
| Remove | How does an item leave the group? | Remove a canceled item from a basket. |
| Membership test | Is this item or key present? | Check whether a customer has already used a promotion. |
| Traverse | How do you visit the stored items? | Print every item on an order. |
| Inspect size | How many items are stored? | Count the orders waiting for collection. |

Not every collection offers every operation, and the method names differ. A stack deliberately limits which item you retrieve next. An array lets you replace an element but does not let you add a new position to that same array. The operations and their rules form a collection's **contract**: the behavior a programmer can rely on.

A **data structure** is an organization of stored information that supports operations. A library collection gives you an already implemented data structure through a public interface of methods and properties. You can use a list before you know how its storage grows, just as you can call `Math.Round` before implementing a rounding algorithm. Later chapters examine the implementation choices behind these operations.

Keep the question of behavior separate from the question of storage. A queue promises a first-in, first-out processing rule. That rule does not require you to know whether a particular implementation uses an array or linked nodes. Conversely, the fact that two collections both store strings does not mean that their access rules are interchangeable.

```

## Collection Families

```{index} collection; families; access pattern
```

An **access pattern** describes how a program usually retrieves and processes its data. Do you know an item's position? Do you know a key that identifies it? Do you only need to know whether it is present? Must items be processed in arrival order?

In the type names below, `T` stands for an element type you choose, such as `string` or `int`. `TKey`, `TValue`, and `TPriority` name the corresponding key, value, and priority types. The examples later in this section use `new` to construct a collection and dot notation to call its operations. First, read the table for the organizing idea behind each family; the next discussion explains generic type arguments before you examine the individual examples.

**Table: An introductory map of .NET collection families.** Adapted from Microsoft's collection-selection guidance, with original business examples and an added priority-queue entry.[^0801_collections-collection-guide][^0801_collections-priority-queue] These eight families are a teaching selection, not Microsoft's exhaustive classification. Sorted variants and collections for specialized settings extend this map.

| Family | Representative type | Main access rule | Business use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array | `T[]`, such as `int[]` | Retrieve by index; length is fixed. | Store one quantity for each of five business days. |
| List | `List<T>` | Retrieve by index; the sequence can grow or shrink. | Build a customer's basket as items are selected. |
| Linked list | `LinkedList<T>` | Follow linked nodes; insert or remove at a known node. | Insert a processing step beside an already located step. |
| Dictionary | `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` | Retrieve a value using its unique key. | Look up stock by product code. |
| Set | `HashSet<T>` | Test membership; equal values occur only once. | Track distinct customers who used a promotion. |
| Stack | `Stack<T>` | Retrieve the most recently added item first. | Keep a history of actions to undo. |
| Queue | `Queue<T>` | Retrieve the earliest added item first. | Process service requests in arrival order. |
| Priority queue | `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>` | Retrieve an item with the lowest priority value first. | Process urgent requests before routine requests. |

The same business process can need several collections. A bookstore might use a dictionary for stock lookup, a list for basket contents, and a queue for orders awaiting service. Choosing one collection does not commit the whole application to that family.

Three distinctions help you read the table. **Position** identifies where an element currently sits in a sequence. **Identity** identifies which entity you mean, such as a product code. **Processing order** determines which waiting item is handled next. Confusing these ideas produces fragile programs: a product code should not silently change because an earlier item was removed from a list.

## Choosing a Collection

```{index} collection selection; duplicate; order; lookup
```

Start with the work the program must do, rather than the longest list of available methods. For a bookstore promotion, suppose the manager asks for four results: the order of product selections, the current stock for a known code, the distinct customers who participated, and the next request to process.

An ordered list preserves selections, including repeated product codes. A dictionary associates a product code with its stock quantity. A set records distinct participating customers. A queue selects the next request if the policy is arrival order; a priority queue is appropriate if a defined priority rule should determine service. These structures can collaborate in one application because they answer different questions.

Use the following questions to explain a choice:

1. **What is one element?** A product code, an integer quantity, or a request is a different unit of information. Define what an entry represents before choosing a type.
2. **How will you retrieve it?** Distinguish an index, an identifying key, a membership test, and a next-item rule.
3. **Do order and duplicates carry information?** Removing duplicates from a transaction history can lose events. Preserving every duplicate in a distinct-customer report can misstate participation.
4. **Does the size change?** Decide whether fixed positions describe the task or whether adding and removing elements is normal work.
5. **What operations must be safe?** Consider missing keys, empty collections, invalid values, and whether another part of the program shares the object.

Performance matters too, but "fast" needs an operation and a situation. A dictionary is designed for lookup by key; it does not make every kind of search or report automatically fast. A linked list can insert beside a known node without shifting a suffix, but finding that node can take traversal. Later chapters develop these costs systematically. Here, explain the behavioral fit first and avoid claims that one family is always best.

Trees and graphs extend the larger study of data structures. They model hierarchies and networks, rather than adding two more standard generic classes named `Tree<T>` and `Graph<T>` to this table. Chapters 17 and 20 teach those structures and their applications. Arrays are developed in Chapter 7; linked structures in Chapter 14; stacks and queues in Chapter 15; priority queues in Chapter 18; and hashing and sets in Chapter 19.

For this chapter's detailed coding and assignments, concentrate on lists and dictionaries. The broader family map should help you recognize alternatives and ask better questions about the data. You do not need the internal mechanics of a hash table or heap to explain why a lookup table and a waiting line have different access rules.

**Guided choice: the daily order desk**

A shop stores five daily sales totals, receives a changing sequence of basket items, looks up stock by product code, and handles requests in arrival order. For each requirement, name the identifying information (position, key, or processing order), select a family, and explain one unsuitable alternative. Then change the requirement: what if urgent requests should go first?

```{dropdown} Reasoning to compare with yours
Five fixed positions fit an array. Basket items fit a list because their number changes and repeated selections can matter. Stock lookup fits a dictionary keyed by product code. Arrival-order service fits a queue; a stack would serve the most recent request first. Urgency suggests a priority queue with an explicitly defined priority policy. These choices follow the operations, not the fact that all four groups contain business data.
```

# Data Collections

An inventory report may need ordered items, a lookup by product ID, or a record of which IDs have already appeared. Arrays are one collection family, but different access rules support different tasks. This chapter compares those families and their shared operations, then develops lists and dictionaries through creation, updates, traversal, missing-data policies, and reference behavior.

- **List**: A `List<T>` stores an ordered sequence that can grow or shrink.
- **Dictionary**: A `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` maps keys to values for fast lookup.
- **Generics**: Generic type parameters keep collections type-safe while making them reusable.
- **Access pattern**: Choosing a collection depends on whether you need order, lookup by key, insertion, removal, or traversal.

## Watch the Suspended Neighbor Loop

Depth-first search is ordinary recursive control flow applied to a graph. A call must remember which neighbor it is considering while a child explores its branch. This connects the suspended calls in Chapter 17 to Chapter 20's cycles and shared destinations. A discovered set avoids repeated discovery; it does not erase the caller's unfinished neighbor loop.

Use the undirected diamond A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, and isolated E. In each array below, the listed neighbor order determines the trace. Watch enter and exit events separately. A vertex is entered once; returning from a child resumes an already active parent rather than entering that parent again.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Enter A depth 0
Enter B depth 1
Enter D depth 2
Enter C depth 3
Exit C
Exit D
Exit B
Exit A
E reached: False

source:
C is first entered from D, not from A. A's neighbor loop has not finished, but C is already discovered by the time A resumes and considers it. C's DFS depth is three although A has a direct edge to C. A first DFS route therefore need not minimize hops.

| Event | Active frames from oldest to newest | What waits in the caller? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enter A | A | A will consider C after B returns |
| Enter B | A,B | B will finish after D returns |
| Enter D | A,B,D | D will finish after C returns |
| Enter C | A,B,D,C | C finds no undiscovered neighbor |
| Exit C | A,B,D | D resumes its neighbor loop |
| Exit D | A,B | B resumes |
| Exit B | A | A sees that C is already discovered |
| Exit A | Empty | Source traversal is complete |

Do not use the number of discovered vertices as the current stack depth. Four vertices have been discovered after C exits, but only three calls remain active at that point. Likewise, a visited neighbor alone is not enough to classify a directed cycle: completed and active destinations have different meanings.

For an undirected graph, a component is the maximal group reachable from any of its members. Keep the discovered set across searches, then start another search from each undiscovered vertex. Starting a new traversal from a vertex that is already discovered would split or duplicate a component.

## Finish One Branch Before Returning to Its Alternatives

Depth-first search follows an unvisited neighbor, completes the exploration reachable through that choice, and then returns to the caller's remaining neighbors. The control pattern connects to tree traversal, but a graph can have shared destinations and cycles. A discovered set prevents following those connections forever.

Use A with neighbors B and C, B connected to D, and C also connected to D. With B considered first, a recursive DFS can enter A, B, D and then C if the adjacency order supplies that route. When the call from D has completed, execution resumes in the suspended neighbor loop of its caller. A plain stack of vertices can provide a valid depth-first exploration policy, but reproducing exact recursive entry/exit timing requires storing enough progress to know which neighbor a suspended frame should consider next.

| Event | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Enter a new vertex | Mark discovered; begin its neighbor sequence |
| Encounter an already discovered vertex | Avoid a second discovery; interpret the edge under the graph model |
| Return from a child | Resume the parent's remaining neighbors |
| Exit a vertex | Its chosen neighbor sequence is complete |

Do not infer a directed cycle merely from seeing an edge to any previously visited vertex. That destination might already have completed. Directed-cycle reasoning distinguishes an active unfinished path from completed exploration. In an undirected graph, the edge back to the parent also needs special treatment. A single Boolean visited flag solves repeated discovery; additional state or parent information may be needed for the specific cycle question.

## Connectivity Depends on Direction

For a symmetric undirected adjacency model, repeated traversals from undiscovered vertices partition the graph into connected components. Every vertex belongs to exactly one such component, and an isolated vertex forms a component by itself. Directed reachability is not symmetric: A may reach B even when B cannot reach A. Repeating ordinary forward searches in arbitrary order does not automatically compute strongly connected components.

Verification can check that each discovered vertex enters/exits once, parent-child call intervals are nested under the recursive model, and every reported reachable vertex has a path from the source. It should not assume that DFS yields minimum-hop paths. BFS has that guarantee under its unweighted model; DFS's first route may be longer.

Then reverse one edge in the chain and identify which reachability claims must be reconsidered. Depth-first search (DFS) follows a branch before returning to another neighbor. Mark before following neighbors: a cycle then leads to an already visited vertex rather than infinite recursion. ## Costs and Contracts

```{index} Costs and Contracts
```

With adjacency lists and expected constant-time dictionary and set operations, a complete traversal takes O(V+E) time: each vertex is discovered once and each stored adjacency is examined once. An undirected edge is stored twice, which changes a constant factor. Visited state, predecessor state, and the queue or recursion stack require O(V) auxiliary space. Matrix traversal instead scans V potential neighbors per visited vertex and can take O(V²). Graph snapshots returned by Vertices and Neighbors protect the stored lists; the strings themselves are immutable. Unknown sources are rejected. The examples do not modify the graph during a search.

## Traversal Verification Contracts

```{index} graph traversal; verification
```

Verify a BFS result by checking that the source has distance zero, each reachable non-source has a predecessor one layer earlier, and every examined edge satisfies the layer bound. Check unreachable vertices separately. A shortest path in edge count need not minimize weighted cost; Chapter 24 supplies Dijkstra’s algorithm for nonnegative weights.

For DFS, check that each reached vertex enters and exits exactly once, every child interval is nested in its parent interval, and cycles do not cause repeated discovery. An explicit stack of suspended neighbor positions reproduces recursive order; a stack that pushes all neighbors at once may produce another order.

## Turn Queue Events into a Traversal Loop

A facilities graph answers which rooms can be reached and how many doorways a shortest route uses. Every edge in this lesson contributes one hop. The queue is not a list of completed rooms; it holds discovered rooms whose neighbors still need examination. This is the queue policy from Chapter 15 applied to the graph model from the preceding sections.

Use directed edges A→B, A→C, B→D and C→D, plus an isolated E. Neighbor order is written explicitly. Begin with A discovered, distance zero and no predecessor. The small program exposes the traversal core; the full graph class and validation examples remain below.

outputs.name: stdout

Discover B: distance 1, from A
Discover C: distance 1, from A
Discover D: distance 2, from B
D hops: 2; E reached: False

source:
Here membership in `distance` also means discovered, so a separate visited set would duplicate that fact. All endpoints are declared in this teaching graph. Production validation of unknown labels is retained in the complete implementation.

| Statement group | Meaning in the trace | Why the order matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dequeue current | Choose the oldest waiting room | Complete this layer before later layers |
| Test distance membership | Skip a previously discovered neighbor | C must not enqueue D a second time |
| Store distance and predecessor | Record the first discovery | A known room has one chosen route witness |
| Enqueue neighbor | Schedule its remaining work | Mark discovery before another parent can find it |

After A, the queue is B,C. After B, it is C,D; D already has distance two and predecessor B. When C examines D, the membership test succeeds and no new queue entry is added. A cycle back to A is harmless for the same reason: A was marked before processing began.

A predecessor map points backwards. For D, following D←B←A gives a reverse route. Reverse those labels to display A→B→D. A missing destination has no such chain; do not create a one-room route and call it reachable. The source itself is a valid one-room route with zero edges.

## Discover a Vertex Once, Then Process Its Neighbors

A delivery graph has edges A-B, A-C, B-D and C-D. Starting at A, how many roads are needed to reach each stop? Breadth-first search answers a minimum-hop question in an unweighted graph. It keeps a queue of discovered vertices whose outgoing neighbors still need examination. Discovery and processing are different events: a vertex can already be known while it is still waiting in the queue.

Mark a vertex discovered when it is enqueued. If you wait until dequeue, both B and C can enqueue D before D is processed. That duplicates work and makes predecessor choices harder to reason about. A visited/discovered set is therefore part of the algorithm's state, not merely an optional speed optimization.

| Processing event | Queue afterward | Newly discovered distances |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initialize A | A | A: 0 |
| Examine A | B, C | B: 1, C: 1 |
| Examine B | C, D | D: 2 |
| Examine C | D | None; D is already known |
| Examine D | Empty | None |

The table assumes that A lists B before C. A different neighbor order can choose another equally short predecessor route, but it does not change the minimum hop distance. Tests that insist on one exact path without specifying neighbor order can reject correct results. State the tie policy separately from the distance claim.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

## Recover a Path from Earlier Layers

When discovering a new vertex v from u, record predecessor[v] = u and distance[v] = distance[u] + 1. Following those predecessor links backward reconstructs a route to the source. Reverse the route to display it from source to destination. The source is a one-vertex route to itself; an unreachable known vertex has no source route. Do not fabricate a destination-only path when no predecessor chain exists.

Why is the distance minimal? The queue processes vertices in nondecreasing discovered distance. All one-hop vertices are discovered from the source before processing can expose a two-hop successor, and the same reasoning repeats layer by layer. The first discovery therefore uses a shortest hop count. This reasoning relies on equal edge contribution, not on geometric closeness or vertex spelling. With arbitrary weights, fewer edges can be more expensive; Chapter 24 treats that different objective.

For adjacency lists, visiting reachable vertices and their incident/outgoing entries costs work proportional to those entries plus vertex bookkeeping. A traversal of one component does not visit all disconnected components by magic. If the task is a full undirected component report, start a new traversal from each still-undiscovered vertex, including isolates.

A representation stores connections; traversal systematically discovers what those connections imply. Start with declared vertices so isolated rooms remain visible. These are minimum edge counts for an unweighted graph; they are not minimum travel times when weights differ.

# Graph Vocabulary and Models

```{index} Vertices and Edges
```

## Vertices and Edges
```{index} graph; vertex; edge; isolated vertex

A graph consists of a set of **vertices** and a set of **edges** connecting them. A vertex models an item; an edge models a relationship. A facilities team might model rooms as vertices and direct passageways as edges. A dependency model might instead use tasks as vertices and prerequisite relationships as edges.

Keep the vertex set separate from the edge set. A room with no modeled passageways is still a vertex. Such an **isolated vertex** has degree zero. If you create vertices only while reading edges, you can silently lose isolated rooms, devices, or customers.

The following office-route model has six vertices and four undirected edges. Labels are symbolic identifiers, not measured physical locations. The diagram expresses the relationships, while the arrays store them.

```text
Lobby -- Hall -- Lab       Remote
          |
        Office -- Storage
```

The drawing is not a floor plan: line lengths do not represent distance, and a crossing in a drawing would not create a new vertex unless the model explicitly added one.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
vertices=6, edges=4
Lobby <-> Hall
Hall <-> Lab
Hall <-> Office
Office <-> Storage
Remote is present even though no edge touches it.

source:
```{index} Directed and Undirected Relationships
```

## Directed and Undirected Relationships
```{index} directed graph; undirected graph; arc; indegree; outdegree

An **undirected edge** represents a two-way relationship. One logical edge between Hall and Lab connects them in both directions. A **directed edge**, also called an arc, has a source and destination; Hall → Lab does not imply Lab → Hall.

Direction depends on the question. A prerequisite arrow from Programming I to Programming II means the first must precede the second. An import arrow might instead mean that the source file depends on the destination file. State the convention before interpreting incoming and outgoing edges.

For directed graphs, **outdegree** counts outgoing edges and **indegree** counts incoming edges. A workflow approval step can have several incoming prerequisites and one outgoing next step.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Request: in=0, out=1
Budget: in=0, out=1
Approve: in=2, out=1
Archive: in=1, out=0
reverse approval edge=False

source: Approve has indegree two and outdegree one. Every directed edge contributes once to the total indegree and once to the total outdegree, so each total equals E, the number of directed edges. In an undirected graph, each ordinary edge contributes one to each endpoint's degree, giving degree sum 2E. These equalities are useful representation checks; they do not prove every edge is the intended one.

```{index} Weights and Model Assumptions
```

## Weights and Model Assumptions
```{index} weighted graph; unweighted graph; edge weight

A **weighted graph** assigns a value to each edge, such as transfer time, cost, capacity, or distance. Define units and the meaning of combination. Walking times can be added along a route. Capacities generally do not add in the same way, so an algorithm that sums weights may answer the wrong business question for that model.

The route examples use nonnegative integer minutes. Zero can represent a rounded transfer time between adjacent work areas. Absence is a different state: no direct route exists. A directed weighted model could give different costs in opposite directions; an undirected one stores one shared cost.

outputs.name: stdout

Lobby <-> Hall: 4 min
Hall <-> Office: 3 min
Office <-> Storage: 0 min
specified route total=7 min

source: This is the cost of one specified route, not a claim that the route is fastest. Negative weights may make sense in some other domains, but this chapter's walking-time contract rejects them. Later algorithms must state their own weight assumptions; a storage representation alone does not make an optimization method valid.

```{index} Neighbors, Degree, and Connectivity
```

## Neighbors, Degree, and Connectivity
```{index} neighbor; degree; connected graph; connected component

Two vertices are **adjacent** when an edge directly connects them. A vertex's neighbors are its adjacent vertices. In the simple undirected model, degree equals the number of distinct neighbors.

```text
Lobby:   Hall
Hall:    Lobby, Lab, Office
Lab:     Hall
Office:  Hall, Storage
Storage: Office
Remote:  (none)
```

Hall has degree three; Remote has degree zero. The sum of these degrees is eight, consistent with four undirected edges. A **connected graph** has a route between every pair of vertices. A **connected component** is a maximal connected group of vertices. Here five rooms form one component and Remote forms another. An isolated vertex is a component of one vertex.

Direct adjacency differs from connectivity. Lobby and Storage have no direct edge, but the model includes the route Lobby, Hall, Office, Storage. A `HasEdge` lookup cannot by itself decide whether some longer route exists. Full reachability algorithms are deferred to Chapter 26.

```{index} Walks, Paths, and Cycles
```

## Walks, Paths, and Cycles
```{index} walk; path; cycle; path length

A **walk** is a sequence in which each consecutive pair is joined by an edge in the required direction. A walk may repeat vertices and edges. A **path** in this chapter is a walk without repeated vertices. A **cycle** is a closed walk with no repeated edges or vertices except its start/end. In a simple undirected graph, it uses at least three edges.

`Lobby, Hall, Office, Storage` is a path of three edges. `Lobby, Hall, Lobby` is a walk, but not a path. `Lobby, Storage` is invalid because it requests a missing direct edge. The sequence's number of edges is one less than its number of listed vertices; its weighted cost is the sum of those edges' weights.

A one-vertex path has zero edges and zero cost if that vertex exists. An empty sequence will be defined as invalid in the route checker later in this chapter. An unknown label is also invalid. These conventions prevent an absent room from being mistaken for a valid isolated room.

**Predict:** add the edge Lab–Office to the diagram. Which degrees change? A cycle Hall, Lab, Office, Hall now exists. Do all vertices become connected? Remote is still isolated. An edge update can change local degree and larger connectivity properties at the same time.

```{index} Simple-Graph Contracts
```

## Simple-Graph Contracts
```{index} simple graph; multigraph; self-loop; graph contract

A **simple graph** has no self-loops and at most one edge between a given pair of vertices. A **self-loop** joins a vertex to itself. A **multigraph** may store several distinct edges between the same endpoints, such as separate transport services. Choose the model that matches the domain before selecting storage.

For an undirected simple graph, `(Hall, Lab)` and `(Lab, Hall)` refer to the same logical edge. A raw set of ordered tuples treats them as different tuples unless you normalize their order. Adjacency storage can instead represent the one edge as two reciprocal entries and count it once.

The complete route graph in the next section adopts an explicit contract: vertex labels use ordinal, case-sensitive equality; vertices are added explicitly; both endpoints must exist; self-loops and negative minutes are rejected; repeated edge assignment replaces its weight; removing a vertex removes every incident edge. An isolate stays present until explicitly removed.

Before implementing, identify what the graph omits. A room-level model might ignore doors, stairs, access permissions, or opening hours. Its routes can support decisions only within those assumptions.

# Adjacency Representations

```{index} Adjacency Matrices
```

## Adjacency Matrices
```{index} adjacency matrix; vertex index; symmetry

An adjacency matrix reserves one cell for each ordered pair of vertices. A row describes outgoing connections from its vertex; a column describes incoming connections to its vertex. Map symbolic labels to dense integer indexes before accessing the array.

For the six-room undirected graph, a Boolean matrix has 36 cells, although only eight are true. Four logical edges appear twice, once in each direction. Its diagonal is false because the model rejects self-loops. An isolated vertex still has a row and column, both empty.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Lobby: 0 1 0 0 0 0
Hall: 1 0 1 1 0 0
Lab: 0 1 0 0 0 0
Office: 0 1 0 0 1 0
Storage: 0 0 0 1 0 0
Remote: 0 0 0 0 0 0

source:
The Hall row is `1 0 1 1 0 0`; the Remote row is all zeros. In an undirected matrix, `[i, j]` equals `[j, i]`. A directed matrix need not be symmetric. Do not infer a reverse arc merely because an undirected example wrote both cells.

Once indexes are known, direct edge lookup reads one cell in O(1) time. Enumerating a vertex's neighbors scans its entire row, Θ(V) time. Adding or removing vertices in a tightly sized matrix can require a new array and remapping many indexes. Keeping spare capacity or inactive indexes changes that tradeoff and needs its own policy.

```{index} Weights and Absence
```

## Weights and Absence
```{index} weighted adjacency matrix; nullable weight; zero-weight edge

A nullable weight matrix separates a missing edge (`null`) from an existing edge with weight zero. Initializing every cell to zero and treating zero as absence would erase valid zero-minute routes. The diagonal remains null under this simple-graph contract; a zero-cost path from a vertex to itself does not imply a stored self-loop.

edge 0-2 exists=False

```{index} Adjacency Collections
```

## Adjacency Collections
```{index} adjacency list; neighbor map; sparse graph

An adjacency list stores each vertex's actual neighbors. The term includes several concrete choices: a list, a set, or a dictionary of neighbor-to-weight pairs. These choices have different lookup and update costs.

A list supports neighbor iteration but must scan to find a particular neighbor, and it can contain duplicates unless insertion checks for them. A hash set supports expected constant-time membership for unweighted edges. A neighbor dictionary supports expected constant-time lookup and weight replacement while keeping one entry per neighbor. All retain explicit entries for isolated vertices.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
Hall: Lab, Lobby
Lab: Hall
Lobby: Hall
Remote: 
Hall-Lab weight=2

source:
In this undirected model, each logical edge has two stored adjacency entries. The space bound is Θ(V + E), since doubling E changes only the constant factor. A directed outgoing adjacency representation stores one entry per arc. Forgetting the reverse entry in an undirected update creates an asymmetric representation of a supposedly symmetric relationship.

Sorting the keys above is a reporting choice, not a hash-table guarantee. The underlying neighbor dictionary does not promise numerical or alphabetical traversal order. Later graph algorithms may produce different valid visit orders when neighbor enumeration order differs.

```{index} Density and Workload Costs
```

## Density and Workload Costs
```{index} graph density; dense graph; representation cost

For a simple undirected graph with V vertices, the maximum number of edges is `V(V - 1) / 2`: choose an unordered pair of distinct endpoints. The directed maximum without loops is `V(V - 1)` because each pair has two possible directions. Density is actual edges divided by the relevant maximum. For fewer than two vertices, this chapter reports density zero to avoid division by zero.

| Operation | Matrix with known indexes | List per vertex | Hash neighbor map |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Storage | Θ(V²) | Θ(V + E) | Θ(V + E) |
| Direct edge lookup | O(1) | O(deg(u)) | Expected O(1) |
| Iterate neighbors of u | Θ(V) | Θ(deg(u)) | Θ(deg(u)) |
| Set edge weight | O(1) | O(deg(u)) to find it | Expected amortized O(1) |
| Add an isolated vertex | May require Θ(V²) copying | Amortized O(1) in a growable indexed collection | Expected amortized O(1) |

Hash bounds assume well-distributed hashing and fixed-cost label operations; growth can make an individual insertion expensive. Label-to-index lookup is additional work for the matrix. The table's update costs describe directed entries; an undirected edge updates two entries with the same asymptotic bound.

outputs.name: stdout
text:
possible edges=1225, density=4.90%
matrix cells=2500, undirected adjacency entries=120

source:
This graph has 60 of 1225 possible edges, about 4.90% density. A matrix reserves 2500 pair cells; adjacency collections store 120 neighbor entries plus 50 vertex entries. These are counts of storage locations, not equal-size bytes. Dictionary objects, hashing, and arrays have different overheads, so small graphs may favor a matrix even when sparse.

Choose by operations as well as density. Frequent pair checks with a fixed dense vertex set favor a matrix; scanning neighbors in a large sparse graph favors adjacency collections. No fixed density cutoff is a universal decision rule.

```{index} A Protected Route Graph
```

## A Protected Route Graph
```{index} graph API; undirected invariant; defensive copy

Encapsulation should protect graph rules, not merely hide a field's name. `RouteGraph` uses private neighbor dictionaries and returns copied arrays for vertices and neighbors. A caller can edit its copy without changing the stored graph. Returning a mutable collection as `IEnumerable` would not protect it: a caller could cast it back to the original collection type.

The contract requires explicit vertices. `SetEdge` checks both endpoints and weight rules before changing either direction. A new logical edge increases EdgeCount once; replacing its weight changes both reciprocal entries without changing EdgeCount. `TryGetWeight` returns false for an absent endpoint or edge, while degree/neighbor queries throw for an unknown vertex so it cannot masquerade as an isolate.

```{index} Removal, Invariants, and Testing
```

## Removal, Invariants, and Testing
```{index} edge removal; vertex removal; degree sum; graph validation

Removing an undirected edge deletes both reciprocal entries and reduces EdgeCount once. Removing a vertex deletes every reverse reference before removing its own dictionary. Its degree tells you how many logical edges disappear. Other vertices stay present even if they become isolated.

Trace removing Hall from the six-room example. Hall's neighbors are Lobby, Lab, and Office. Remove Hall from each of those neighbor maps, subtract three from EdgeCount, and delete Hall. Five vertices and one edge remain; Lobby and Lab are now isolates, Office–Storage remains, and Remote is unchanged. Removing Hall again returns false.

The representation invariant requires every neighbor label to name an existing vertex, no self-loops, nonnegative weights, equal reverse weights, and degree sum `2 * EdgeCount`. `IsValid` checks those rules in expected Θ(V + E) time. It still cannot prove that the data matches the intended floor plan, so compare edge membership and weights with an independent model too.

With neighbor hashes, `RemoveEdge` takes expected O(1) time. `RemoveVertex(u)` takes expected O(deg(u)) time because it removes a reference at each neighbor. The code does not mutate u's neighbor map while enumerating it; it changes the distinct maps belonging to those neighbors. Self-loops are rejected, so a reverse map cannot be the same map being enumerated.

`Degree` reads a stored dictionary count in expected O(1). `Neighbors` copies deg(u) entries, so it takes Θ(deg(u)) time and space. `Vertices` copies V labels. Defensive copying has a cost, but keeps callers from bypassing update rules.

## String Interpolation

The `$` character identifies a string literal as an **interpolated string**. An interpolated
string is a string literal that might contain interpolation expressions. When an
interpolated string is resolved to a result string, the compiler replaces items with
interpolation expressions by the string representations of the expression results.
String interpolation provides a more readable, convenient syntax to format strings.
To identify a string literal as an interpolated string, prepend it with the `$` symbol.

A business value has a meaning before it has a C# type. A count of delivered packages is a whole number; a quoted price may need decimal fractions; a product code is text even when it consists of digits. Choosing a type is therefore a modeling decision, not a search for the smallest box that happens to fit today's example. Start with the allowed values and operations. Ask whether fractional values make sense, whether leading zeros matter, and whether the quantity can exceed a chosen numeric range.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
